title: Your first ten minutes
summary: Create a project, add a server, repository or SBOM, see what it found, turn on alerts and invite people; then the Dashboard's setup checklist.
keywords: setup set up onboarding first run welcome checklist invite invitation getting started quiet first scan
text:
A new organisation's administrators start in **Set up Stackurity**. Each step can be skipped. Afterwards the Dashboard shows a setup checklist, with a few more steps, until an administrator hides it. Installations that already have assets never see it.

1. **Create a project.** A name, and a description if you like. Use a project for a product, a client, an environment or a team.
2. **Add a server or repo.** **A Linux server**: one install command, first results in about 2 minutes. **A code repository**: a token for your CI and a GitHub Actions step (or the `stackurity scan` command), first results on the next CI run. **Upload an SBOM**: a CycloneDX or SPDX file, first results in under a minute. Whatever you add here lands in the project.
3. **First check.** The page counts what has arrived as it happens: agent connected, components found, issues found, fixes recommended. Vulnerability data is downloaded for the software found; until it has synced, the page says how many components wait for it.
4. **Review fixes.** "Your first check is done": assets, components, issues and coverage, with a link to the top recommended fix.
5. **Choose alerts.** Slack (**Add to Slack**, or a webhook) or email. Choose what to send right away (urgent issues, all new issues, or nothing) and a daily or weekly summary (or none). They cover this project only; fine-tune them later in [Integrations](/integrations).
6. **Invite your team.** By email: they see this project with the permission you choose (or more, if you add it). They get a link that works once, for 7 days.

## A quiet first scan

Connecting an asset never sets off alerts for what it already had. You get one message, for example "commmerceblog connected: 1,676 packages checked, 412 issues found, 3 fixes need you". Its existing issues raise no urgent alert, no Jira issue, no escalation and no overdue reminder, and summaries count them as found when it connected, not as new. Issues found after that alert as usual.

## Invitations

- With an email channel under **Integrations**, the link is emailed through that mail server. Without one, the link is shown once for you to copy and send.
- An invitation says what they will see, like **Add user**: all projects and assets with one permission, or specific projects and assets, each with its own. A project's **Invite** starts with that project; **People ▸ Users ▸ Invite by email** starts with nothing chosen.
- Someone new creates their account from the link and sees what the invitation gives. Someone with an account signs in first, as the invited email address. Someone already in your organisation gets the access at once, without a link.
- Accepting never changes a role someone already has in your organisation, and keeps a higher role they already had on a project or asset.
- What it gives is checked again when they accept: a project archived, or an asset deleted or merged, since you sent it is skipped, and the page tells them. If nothing is left, the link does not work until you send a new invitation.
- Inviting someone again replaces their open invitation. **People ▸ Users** lists every invitation, and a project's page the ones that include it; either can withdraw one that was not used yet.

Note: Running the server yourself? See the install guide (docs/install.md) for the first start, the setup token and backups.

## The checklist on the Dashboard

Administrators see **Finish setting up** on the Dashboard, with how far you have got ("3 of 8 done") and a bar. Each step says why it is worth doing and what you get once it is done, and its button opens the page that does it. A step is ticked from what exists in the workspace, so doing it somewhere else counts too. If a step could not be checked just now, it says so instead of showing a tick.

| Step | Why | Ticked when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connect your first server | See every package your servers run, and which have known vulnerabilities. | At least one server reports. |
| Add your source repositories | Catch vulnerable libraries in the code, before they reach a server. | At least one repository is scanned. |
| Turn on vulnerability alerts | New urgent issues reach Slack or email without anyone opening the Dashboard. | An alert rule is on. |
| Set who owns what | Each issue reaches the right person or team without being forwarded. | At least one owner rule exists ([People ▸ Owners](/people/owners)). |
| Set how issues are prioritised and fixed | Priorities and fix deadlines match how your team works. | The [risk policy](/settings/risk-policy) has been saved, or (Pro) an automatic-fix policy exists. |
| Invite your team | The people who fix things see their own issues. | Someone was invited, or the organisation has another member. |
| Connect an AI assistant | Ask what is installed and what to upgrade, in plain words. | An assistant was connected. |
| Set up two-factor sign-in | A leaked password alone cannot open your admin account. | Your account has a passkey or an authenticator app. |

While there is no project yet, **Create a project** comes first. On Community, the policy step also shows that automatic fixes are part of Stackurity Pro; the step is ticked by the risk policy alone. Once every step is done, **Dismiss** removes the checklist; **Hide the checklist** removes it before then. Either hides it for every administrator in the workspace.

title: Connect an AI assistant
summary: Ask Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini CLI or Replit what is installed, what is vulnerable and what to upgrade.
keywords: ask stackurity in-app assistant chat panel ai assistant claude chatgpt cursor vs code copilot claude code windsurf gemini cli replit mcp connector model context protocol oauth connected assistants allow changes
text:
Stackurity is an MCP server: an AI assistant can read your inventory, issues and fixes as you, and, if you allow it, make changes for you, such as assigning or snoozing issues.

1. Open [Integrations ▸ AI assistants](/integrations/ai-assistants) and copy the address shown there.
2. Click your assistant's card and follow its steps. Cursor, VS Code and Replit have an install button; the others take the address as a custom connector or MCP server.
3. Sign in to Stackurity when the assistant asks. Choose the organisation and what it can see. Tick **Allow changes** only if it should make changes for you. Click **Allow**.

**Connected assistants**, on the same page, lists the assistants you allowed. Turn **Allow changes** on or off there, or click **Disconnect** to stop one at once.

Note: On a server you run yourself, assistants can sign in only once `STACKURITY_BASE_URL` is set to the server's public https:// address. Until then, the page shows how to run `stackurity mcp` on your own computer instead.

## Ask Stackurity, inside the dashboard

Where your organisation has turned it on, the **Ask** button at the top of every page (Alt+K) opens an assistant that answers from your Stackurity data, with links to the issues, assets and fixes it used. It reads only what you can see, and changes nothing. The page you have open is its context; click **(remove)** to ask without it.

An answer leads with a short **Recommendation**. **Why**, **Evidence** and **Alternatives and trade-offs** open on a click; **Data gaps** (what it could not check) starts open. Advisory ids and the issues and assets it names link to their pages, and **What Ask looked at**, under each answer, lists the lookups it made. A how-to answer ("How do I add a server?") is the steps from the Help article, with buttons to the page where you do it (**Open Add server →**) and to the article. Nothing in an answer is done for you: make any change on the linked pages.

Before your first question it shows where your questions go (with Anthropic's API, to Anthropic in the United States) and what is sent: your question, the page you have open and the data the assistant reads, without colleagues' names or email addresses. Your conversations are kept 30 days (backups up to about 60), only you can read them, and **History** lets you delete them. Answers can be wrong: check the linked pages.

Note: Admins turn it on or off, see this month's use and delete everyone's conversations (without reading them) under [Integrations ▸ AI assistants](/integrations/ai-assistants).

title: What Stackurity does
summary: An inventory of what runs where, matched against vulnerability and end-of-life data, grouped into actions.
text:
Stackurity keeps an inventory of the software on your servers, repositories, container images and cloud services. It checks that inventory against public vulnerability data (OSV, CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list) and end-of-life dates (endoflife.date), and tells you what to fix first.

## How the pieces fit

1. **Collect.** A small read-only agent on each server, a CI step for each repository, or a server-side integration reports what is installed. Nothing is changed on the server.
2. **Evaluate.** Every installed package is compared with the advisories for its ecosystem. A match is a **finding**.
3. **Prioritise.** Each finding gets a priority (P1–P4) from its severity, whether it is being exploited, the environment and exposure. Rules in the [risk policy](/help/risk-policy) decide which are **SOS**.
4. **Group into fixes.** [Fixes](/help/action-plan) turns thousands of findings into a handful of jobs, such as “Install available security updates (917 issues)”. The **Dashboard** shows the few that need you now.
5. **Alert and track.** Findings of the same vulnerability for the same team form an **incident**; incidents are sent to Slack, Teams, email or webhooks.
6. **Verify.** The next collection shows the new versions and the findings resolve on their own.

## Finding your way

| Place | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | The landing page after you sign in, in four bands: **Security posture** (urgent and high-priority issues, known exploited, issues past their fix-by date, assets reporting, leaked keys to rotate, what was not checked and, for admins, secrets and credentials), **Needs your attention** (open SOS incidents, issues overdue or due today, approvals waiting, assets that stopped reporting; one button each), **Recommended actions** (the fixes to do first) and **Security trends** (issues opened against fixed per week, the 30-day open-issue line, deadlines met, and open issues by priority). Every number opens the list it counts. |
| Security | What to do and what is wrong. **Fixes**: every fix, one card per change, most urgent first. **All issues**: each finding with filters. **Leaked keys**, **Automatic fixes** (the upgrades Stackurity applies for you, Pro), **Incidents** and **Checks** (Check again and their results). |
| Environment | What you run. **Assets** (servers, repositories, images and cloud services, and **Identity conflicts** when there are some), **Components** (and updates available), **Projects** and **Coverage** (with **Data sources**, the vulnerability feeds). |
| Governance | What was decided and proved. **Approvals** (requests to ignore issues) and **Reports and audit**: remediation outcomes, the evidence report and the audit log. |
| Administration | How Stackurity is set up. **Integrations** (everything Stackurity connects to, the delivery log, stored credentials, API tokens, AI assistants and plugins), **People** (users, teams and owner rules), **Settings** (risk policy, fix grouping, VEX, automatic fix policies, plan and usage, single sign-on and jobs) and **Admin** (for instance administrators: workspaces, platform health, coverage gaps, stack packs, the licence and what's new). |

The sidebar shows only what your role can open: People and Projects need the admin role (security users get their projects' notifications), Admin is for instance administrators. Each group heading opens and closes its items; the group of the page you are on opens by itself, and a closed group shows a count when something inside waits for you. **Collapse** at the bottom narrows the sidebar to icons. On a phone the menu is a bar at the bottom: Dashboard, Fixes, Assets and **More** (the other places by group, Help and feedback). Your workspace is at the top left, search in the middle, and your account menu (email, role, help, feedback, log out) at the top right.

**Search** (press `/` or Ctrl+K, ⌘K on a Mac, anywhere) first lists the **pages, settings and help articles** whose name or a word people use for them matches (type `sso`, `invite` or `api token` to jump straight there; only pages you can open are shown). It also finds vulnerability and advisory ids, packages (optionally with a version, such as `openssl 3.0.2`), assets, teams and people. Press Enter for the full results page. It starts with an **Overview**: how many matching components are installed, in how many versions and on how many assets, and how many open issues are critical or urgent (P1); select a figure to open that list. Then come **Components** (open one for every installed version and the assets it is on), **Vulnerabilities** (CVEs and other issues on your assets, with their severity), **Advisories** (public advisories that match but affect nothing here), then teams and people.

Note: Stackurity runs on your own server and sends no telemetry. The only outbound calls are to the vulnerability feeds, your Git hosts and registries, the notification channels you configure, and [feedback](/help/feedback) when you send it.

title: The daily workflow
summary: Open the Dashboard, do the top fix, let the next check confirm it.
text:
You don't need to read individual findings to make progress. Work from actions, not findings.

1. Open the **Dashboard**. **Security posture** says what is dangerous right now; **Needs your attention** lists what can't wait, each with one button; **Recommended actions** are the most urgent fixes, SOS first, then highest priority, then the number of issues each clears, each with the assets it touches and its effort. All of them are under [Fixes](/fixes). **Security trends**, at the bottom, says whether you are fixing issues faster than they appear.
2. Click **How to fix** on the top card. The fix page says what and why in one sentence, where (the asset and files), and how: the command or upgrade to make, with a **Copy** button and a warning for major upgrades.
3. Do the work on the server, then reboot if the asset shows **Reboot pending** (patched packages protect nothing until the process or kernel restarts).
4. Press **I applied this** on the fix page. Its issues go to **In progress** and Stackurity asks for a fresh report. It never closes an issue by itself.
5. The agent on the server reports within about a minute (agents 0.7 and newer ask every minute). The fix page then says **Passed**, **Partly fixed** (with what is left) or **Still open**. See [Check again](/help/check-again).
6. Fixed issues close on their own. An issue that comes back later is flagged **Regressed** (see [Regressed issues](/help/regressed)).

When a fix can't be applied yet, record why: **Snooze** it until a date or until a fix ships, or **Ignore** it with a reason, a scope and an expiry (see [Snooze and ignore](/help/exceptions) and [Ignore issues](/help/ignore-issues)). Engineers and viewers use **Ask to ignore**, which goes to the [approval inbox](/help/approvals).

Recommended actions also says how many issues it does not show and why (no fix in the standard updates yet, kernels that are not running, assets that are not production, lower priority, snoozed or ignored). Every number is a link to the list it counts. "No fix in the standard updates" means no fixed version is published yet, or the vendor publishes it only in a paid support subscription such as Ubuntu Pro; the fix page says what to do meanwhile.

Words with a dotted underline (SOS, incident, issue, fix) show their meaning when you point at them; the [Glossary](/help/glossary) has the rest. Under the title, **vulnerability data updated** says when the newest data source last synced. A warning appears there when a source is out of date or failing; open [Data sources](/intelligence) to see which (see [Coverage, Intelligence feeds and gaps](/help/coverage-intelligence)).

For alerts, someone on the team should check [Incidents](/incidents) (under **Security**) daily and acknowledge new ones, so escalations don't fire.

title: Glossary
summary: Asset, component, finding, unique vulnerability, incident, action, SOS, KEV, EPSS, P1–P4, Ubuntu Pro, idle kernel, coverage, evidence.
keywords: terms definitions vocabulary
text:
| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Asset | Something that runs software: a host (server or VM), a repository, a container image, an application, a managed cloud service, or an SBOM. |
| Component | A package or library with a version, e.g. `openssl 1.1.1f` or `lodash 4.17.15`. One component can appear on many assets. |
| Finding | One vulnerability (or end-of-life issue) on one installed component on one asset. Kernels are the exception: the packages of one installed kernel version (image, modules, tools) share one finding per CVE, shown on the kernel image, and kernel headers get none. |
| Unique vulnerability | A distinct CVE or advisory, however many packages it affects. This is the number people usually mean by “how many vulnerabilities”. |
| Fix (fix group) | A set of findings that one piece of work resolves, such as installing security updates or upgrading the OS release. Earlier versions called it an action. See [Fixes](/help/action-plan). |
| Issue | The word the dashboard uses for a finding. |
| Snooze | Hide an issue until a date (stored as the **suppressed** state). See [Exceptions](/help/exceptions). |
| Incident | Findings with the same vulnerability on assets owned by the same team, plus system problems (a stale feed, a server whose agent stopped reporting). Notifications are sent per incident. |
| Priority (P1–P4) | How urgent a finding is, from a score: severity or CVSS, plus known exploitation, internet exposure, production, asset criticality and so on. P1 is the most urgent. Each priority has an acknowledge and fix deadline. |
| SOS | A finding that matches one of the SOS rules in the risk policy, e.g. “known exploited in production”. SOS findings ignore quiet hours. |
| KEV | CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue: vulnerabilities attackers are actually using. |
| EPSS | FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the daily probability that a CVE is exploited in the next 30 days. Shown with each issue; at or above the risk policy's threshold it raises the priority. |
| Ubuntu Pro / ESM | Canonical's paid subscription for commercial use (free for limited personal use) that publishes security fixes for releases past standard support and for the universe repository. Findings marked “no free fix” have a fixed build only there; the recommended action stays the free one: upgrade to a supported release, or install the update when Ubuntu publishes it. SUSE LTSS is treated the same way. |
| Idle kernel | A kernel version that is installed but not running. Its vulnerabilities can't be exploited until it is booted, so they get a low priority and the action is to remove old kernels. |
| Reboot pending | The host runs older code than is installed (the distro's reboot flag, or a newer kernel than the running one). |
| Coverage | What each collector checked, skipped or could not read. Findings only cover what was checked. |
| Not checked | A component that was not checked for vulnerabilities, split by who acts: **needs you** (its version could not be read, or the agent may not read the application's files; each says what to do), **Stackurity doesn't support yet** (no vulnerability data for its ecosystem or distribution; nothing for you to do), **resolves on its own** (vulnerability data not synced yet) or **no published advisories** (nothing is known against that release; not counted). It is never treated as clean, and the asset's Inventory tab marks it. |
| Coverage state | How far an asset's findings can be trusted: Healthy and recently evaluated, Stale intelligence, Failed collection, Unsupported, Partially evaluated or Awaiting verification. Shown on the asset page with the reasons. |
| Evidence report | A printable patch-management summary for a period, for audits. |
| Exception | A finding that was suppressed or risk-accepted by a security user, with a reason, optional mitigation and an expiry date. |

title: Send feedback to the Stackurity team
summary: Report an issue, request a feature or ask a question from inside the app, with screenshots if they help, and follow it in My feedback.
keywords: feedback bug issue report feature request idea suggestion question contact support screenshot attachment video reference my feedback status
text:
1. Open your account menu (the round button with your initial, top right) and click **Send feedback**. On a phone it is also under **More** in the bottom bar.
2. Choose **Issue**, **Feature request** or **Question**.
3. Write a description (up to 5,000 characters).
4. Optionally click **Add files** to attach screenshots, a screen recording or a PDF.
5. Your email is filled in so the team can reply; clear it to send without one.
6. Click **Send feedback**. You see “Thanks — your reference is FB-123.” with your item's reference number.

## Attachments

- Up to 3 files: PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF images, MP4 or WebM videos, and PDFs.
- Images and PDFs may be 10 MB each, videos 50 MB each, and 90 MB together.
- The server checks each file's content, not just its name, and refuses anything else.
- Images have their metadata (such as the location a photo was taken, and the camera) removed before they are sent. Videos and PDFs are sent as they are: a video recorded on a phone can carry where it was recorded.

Note: Screenshots may contain your data and will be sent to the Stackurity team. Crop or blur anything you don't want to share (host names, findings, emails) before attaching.

## What is sent

- The type of feedback, your description and any attachments.
- Your email address, only if it is in the form when you send.
- The path of the page you were on, such as `/findings/17`, without search terms or filters.
- Your browser and window size, such as “Chrome 131 on macOS, 1440x900”.
- The Stackurity version and edition.

Nothing else: no findings, asset, host or workspace names (unless they are in your description or a screenshot), and not this installation's address. Your Stackurity server sends it, not your browser, and each send is recorded in the [audit log](/audit) as `feedback.send`.

## Follow up in My feedback

Each item gets a reference number such as `FB-123`; quote it if you write to the team about it. **My feedback** in your account menu (on a phone, under **More**) lists what you sent with its status: Received, Under review, In progress, Fixed (waiting for release), Released (with the version), Won't fix or Duplicate, and any note from the team. Statuses are checked with the Stackurity team's server when you open the page; if it can't be reached, the page says so and shows the last status it knew.

Note: Operators can send feedback somewhere else, or turn it off, with `STACKURITY_FEEDBACK_URL`. When it is off, the menu item is not shown.

For a security vulnerability in Stackurity itself, follow the security policy (SECURITY.md in the repository) instead of using feedback.

title: Add a server
summary: Create a one-time install command in the dashboard and run it on the new Linux or Windows server or Mac. Admins only.
keywords: add server new server install command enroll enrollment code curl sudo agent linux systemd windows powershell service onboarding project missing not showing
text:
The quickest way to add a Linux or Windows server is a one-time install command. It installs the same read-only `stackurity` agent as a manual install, without creating a token or setting up a service by hand.

1. Open [Assets](/assets) and click **Add server** (admins only).
2. If you use projects, choose the **Project** the server goes into. The project you are looking at in the project picker, or your only project, is already chosen. The server and the apps found on it are added to it, so everyone working on the project sees them. A server in no project is seen only by people who see all projects.
3. Optionally enter a **Label** (e.g. `web servers`) and an **Environment** (e.g. `production`; production counts towards priority).
4. **Also check websites and apps on this server** is ticked by default: the agent looks in /srv, /var/www, /opt, /app and home directories for sites and apps (including WordPress sites, whose WordPress core version is read from `wp-includes/version.php` and checked for end of life and for missing security releases on its branch; its plugins and themes are listed with their latest release on wordpress.org, but their vulnerabilities are not matched yet), and lists the libraries they use: what npm, pip and Composer installed, and front-end libraries such as jQuery or Bootstrap that a site loads from a CDN or keeps a copy of (copies WordPress itself maintains are reported with inferred confidence, so their issues show as needs validation). In a compiled app (a webpack, Vite or Next.js build, or a Flutter web build) it reports the libraries whose licence banner, version constant or source map names their release, and the Flutter engine revision; the rest of a bundle cannot be identified, and the app says so under coverage instead of showing no components. It only reads. Under **Application directories**, add apps that live somewhere else, one per line, e.g. `/data/shop`.
5. Under **Options**, set how many servers the code can enroll (default 1) and how long it is valid (default 24 hours).
6. Click **Create install command**, choose the **Linux** or **Windows** tab, and copy the command. The code in it is shown only once.
7. On Linux, run it as a user with sudo. On Windows, run it in PowerShell opened with **Run as administrator**.

Install command for Linux:
```
curl -fsSL https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent.sh | sudo STACKURITY_ENROLL_CODE=… sh
```

Install command for Windows (PowerShell as administrator):
```
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072; $env:STACKURITY_ENROLL_CODE = '…'; irm https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent.ps1 | iex
```

## What it does on Linux

- Downloads the agent from your Stackurity server (Linux amd64 or arm64) and verifies its checksum.
- Creates an unprivileged `stackurity` user and enrolls the server with the code.
- Installs a hardened systemd service that reports every 6 hours. Running the command again upgrades the agent.
- The agent only reads what is installed. It never installs or changes software.

## What it does on Windows

See [Add a Windows server](/help/windows-hosts).

## What the agent reads and sends

- **Reads and sends:** the server's name and machine ID, its operating system version, packages and installed programs, and on Linux and macOS runtimes such as Node.js or Python installed outside the package manager: their names, versions and where they were found (for rpm packages also the ID of the key that signed each, and the enabled module streams), not file contents. Websites and apps and their libraries (on by default), and the images of running Docker containers (only if ticked).
- **Keys and passwords** written into those apps' files are reported by file, line, setting and kind of key, with a fingerprint and, for a key, a masked preview such as `sk_live_…4f2a`. The value itself never leaves the server. `--no-leaks` (or `STACKURITY_NO_LEAKS=true`) turns this off.
- **Changes nothing:** it never installs, removes or changes software. Automatic fixing is a separate paid feature (Pro) for Linux that needs the agent to run as root with `--remediate`, a token an admin binds to that server, and an allowlist file on the server itself; the install command never turns it on.
- **Runs as** its own unprivileged account: `stackurity` on Linux, `_stackurity` on macOS, `NT SERVICE\StackurityAgent` on Windows. Only the install needs root or an administrator. Checking Docker containers gives it the Docker socket, which is equivalent to root.
- **Connects to** this Stackurity server only, over HTTPS unless you allow plain HTTP: no telemetry and no update checks. Each pull request checks this by running the agent against a server that records every connection.
- **Reports** when it starts and every 6 hours. In between, about once a minute, it asks the server whether someone pressed **Check again**.
- `stackurity agent --once --output -` prints what it collects without sending it.

## Remove the agent

Remove the agent on Linux:
```
sudo systemctl disable --now stackurity-agent
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/stackurity-agent.service /usr/local/bin/stackurity
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm -rf /etc/stackurity
sudo userdel stackurity
```

Remove the agent on macOS:
```
curl -fsSL https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent-macos.sh | sudo STACKURITY_UNINSTALL=1 sh
```

Remove the agent on Windows (PowerShell as administrator):
```
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072; $env:STACKURITY_UNINSTALL = '1'; irm https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent.ps1 | iex
```

**Add server** shows these commands with your server's address. The server stays under **Assets** until you delete it there, and its token works until you revoke it under **Integrations → API tokens**.

## Requirements

- Linux with systemd, and root or sudo; or 64-bit Windows Server 2016 or later (or Windows 10 or 11), and PowerShell run as administrator.
- Outbound HTTPS from the server to the Stackurity dashboard.

Warning: If the dashboard is reached over plain HTTP (not localhost), the installer refuses unless `STACKURITY_ALLOW_HTTP=1` is added, and the command shown includes it. Prefer HTTPS, or [an SSH tunnel](/help/ssh-tunnel) to a local port.

## Afterwards

- The server appears under **Assets** within a minute, in the project you chose; applications appear as their own assets linked to it. A server already enrolled in no project: switch the project picker to **All projects**, open **Assets → Not in a project**, then add it to a project from the project's page.
- Unused codes are listed under **Pending install codes** on the same page until they expire or are used up. **Revoke** one you no longer need; servers that already enrolled keep reporting.
- For many servers at once (cloud-init, Ansible, Terraform, an SSH loop or DigitalOcean), see [Add many servers](/help/add-many-servers).
- For a Mac, see [Add a Mac](/help/macos-hosts). To install by hand, see [Add a Linux server manually](/help/add-linux-server), [Add a Windows server](/help/windows-hosts) and docs/install.md.

title: Add many servers
summary: Create a fleet code for up to 1,000 servers and install with cloud-init, Ansible, Terraform or an SSH loop. List DigitalOcean droplets and see which are not covered. Admins only.
where: Environment › Assets › Add server › For many servers
keywords: fleet many servers bulk rollout cloud-init user data ansible playbook terraform user_data ssh loop digitalocean droplets tag enrollment code
text:
A **fleet code** is an install code made for a rollout: you choose how many servers it may enroll (up to 1,000) and how long it is valid (up to 90 days). Each server exchanges it for its own collector token, so no long-lived token goes into user data, a playbook or a script.

1. Open [Assets](/assets), click **Add server**, then **For many servers**.
2. Enter **How many servers** and **Valid for (days)**, and optionally a label, project, environment and application directories.
3. Click **Create fleet code**. The code is shown once, with snippets for cloud-init, Ansible, Terraform and an SSH loop. Copy the one you need.
4. Run it. Servers that already have the agent skip enrollment, so running a snippet twice is safe.

## Watching the rollout

- **Fleet codes** on the same page lists each code with how many servers it has enrolled. **Show servers** lists which hosts used it, from which address and when.
- **Revoke** stops a code at once. Servers that already enrolled keep reporting; revoke their tokens under **Integrations → API tokens** if needed (the list shows each token's prefix).
- Up to 60 servers enroll per minute with one code. Servers over the limit wait and try again on their own.

Warning: Treat a fleet code like a password until it expires: anyone who has it can enroll machines into your organisation. Keep the count and expiry close to what you need, and revoke it when the rollout is done. Cloud user data can be read from inside the machine and is kept in Terraform state.

## DigitalOcean

- Under **DigitalOcean**, add an API token with read access to droplets (a custom token with `droplet:read` is enough). It is stored encrypted and never shown again.
- The list shows each droplet with its region and tags, and whether an agent reports from it (matched by hostname, or by the address it enrolled from).
- Tick the droplets to cover and click **Create commands**: you get a fleet code sized for them, an SSH command for each droplet, and one loop for all of them.
- For new droplets, add the cloud-init snippet as user data when you create them and give them a tag so the list shows them. A tag alone installs nothing.

Note: Stackurity does not install on droplets itself. DigitalOcean has no API to run a command on an existing droplet, and connecting to your servers over SSH would give Stackurity root access to them. You run the commands with the access you already have.

title: Add a Linux server manually
summary: Create a collector token, install the agent binary, run it as a systemd service. Repeat for each server.
keywords: add server second server more servers agent install host token systemd collector manual
text:
Note: Most servers are easier to add with a one-time install command: see [Add a server](/help/add-server). Use these steps when you can't run the installer.

Every server runs the same small `stackurity` agent. It reads `/etc/os-release` and the dpkg, rpm or apk database, plus runtimes installed outside the package manager, and sends the list to Stackurity. It runs as an unprivileged user and never installs or changes software.

## 1. Create a collector token (once)

1. Go to **Integrations ▸ API tokens**.
2. Under **Create token**, enter a name such as `servers`, choose role **collector (submit observations only)**, and leave the expiry empty (or set hours).
3. Click **Create token** and copy the token (it starts with `stk_`). It is shown only once.
4. You can use one collector token for all servers, or one per server so you can revoke them separately. Only admins can create collector tokens.

Admins can also create one on the server: `docker compose exec stackurity stackurity admin create-token --name servers` (add `--ttl 8760h` for a one-year expiry).

## 2. Get the agent binary

- From a release, when one is published: download `stackurity_<version>_linux_amd64` (or `_linux_arm64`) and verify `SHA256SUMS` with cosign as described in docs/security-audit.md.
- Or copy it from your Stackurity server's container (same CPU architecture; the binary is static): `docker compose cp stackurity:/usr/local/bin/stackurity ./stackurity`, then `scp` it to the new server.
- Or build it from source: `make build` produces `bin/stackurity` (needs Go and Node.js).

## 3. Install it on the new server (as root)

Install the agent:
```
install -m 0755 stackurity /usr/local/bin/stackurity
useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin stackurity
install -d -m 0750 -o stackurity /etc/stackurity
printf '%s\n' 'stk_...' > /etc/stackurity/token
chown stackurity /etc/stackurity/token && chmod 600 /etc/stackurity/token
```

## 4. Run it every 6 hours with systemd

systemd unit:
```
# /etc/systemd/system/stackurity-agent.service
[Unit]
Description=Stackurity inventory agent
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=stackurity
Environment=STACKURITY_SERVER=https://stackurity.example.com
Environment=STACKURITY_TOKEN_FILE=/etc/stackurity/token
Environment=STACKURITY_ENVIRONMENT=production
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/stackurity agent --interval 6h
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

- `STACKURITY_SERVER` is the dashboard URL. If the server is only reachable over SSH, see [Connect over an SSH tunnel](/help/ssh-tunnel).
- `STACKURITY_ENVIRONMENT` (or `--environment`) labels the asset, e.g. `production` or `staging`. Production counts towards priority and SOS.
- `--interval` sets how often it reports (default `6h`).
- With `ProtectHome=yes` the agent can't see per-user installs such as `~/.nvm`; use `ProtectHome=read-only` to include them.

Start it:
```
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now stackurity-agent
journalctl -u stackurity-agent -n 20
```

## 5. Check it arrived

1. The log shows a line like `asset 7: 1834 observations stored (collection 12, 0 removed), new asset`.
2. Open **Assets**. The server is listed under its hostname.
3. Open it, click **Edit** under *Ownership & context* and set the owner team, criticality and whether it is internet exposed. These change priorities.
4. Findings appear within a few minutes; the first download of a vulnerability feed for a new OS can take longer.

## Troubleshooting

- `stackurity diagnostics --server https://… --token-file /etc/stackurity/token` checks connectivity, authentication and version.
- `stackurity agent --once -o -` prints exactly what would be sent, without sending it.
- “no token: set STACKURITY_TOKEN or --token-file”: the token file path is wrong or unreadable by the agent user.
- If two servers share a cloned machine-id they can merge into one asset; an admin resolves that under [Identity conflicts](/help/admin-tools).

title: Connect a server over an SSH tunnel
summary: When the dashboard isn't exposed to the internet, run the agent through a restricted SSH port forward (useful when the server has no public address).
keywords: tunnel ssh port forward private network firewall
text:
If Stackurity listens only on the server's localhost (for example on `127.0.0.1:8180`), an agent on another machine can reach it through an SSH port forward. Use a dedicated account that can do nothing except forward that one port.

1. On the Stackurity server, create a tunnel-only user with no shell, and add the agent host's public key to its `authorized_keys` with restrictions: `restrict,port-forwarding,permitopen="127.0.0.1:8180" ssh-ed25519 AAAA… agent@host`.
2. On the agent host, create an SSH key for the tunnel (no passphrase, readable only by root).
3. Add a systemd unit that keeps the tunnel open (below).
4. Point the agent at the local end: `Environment=STACKURITY_SERVER=http://127.0.0.1:8180`, and add `After=stackurity-tunnel.service` and `Wants=stackurity-tunnel.service` to the agent unit.
5. Start both units and check the asset appears under **Assets**.

Tunnel unit:
```
# /etc/systemd/system/stackurity-tunnel.service
[Unit]
Description=SSH tunnel to Stackurity
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/ssh -N -i /root/.ssh/stackurity_tunnel \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:8180:127.0.0.1:8180 stackurity-tunnel@stackurity.example.com
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Note: Traffic inside the tunnel is plain HTTP to localhost, which is fine because SSH encrypts it. Don't open the dashboard port in the firewall for this.

title: Add a Windows server
summary: One PowerShell command installs the read-only agent as a Windows service. It reads the OS build and installed programs from the registry.
keywords: windows powershell service install command enroll registry irm iex administrator uninstall scheduled task
text:
On Windows the agent reads the OS build and the installed programs as “Apps & features” shows them. It only reads. Windows Update hotfixes and Microsoft Store apps are reported as unsupported coverage for now; remediation and application directories are Linux-only.

1. Open [Assets](/assets), click **Add server** and create an install command (admins only), as in [Add a server](/help/add-server).
2. Choose the **Windows** tab and copy the command. The code in it is shown only once.
3. On the server, open PowerShell with **Run as administrator** and paste the command.
4. Check the server appears under **Assets** with its Windows release and build.

Install command (PowerShell as administrator):
```
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072; $env:STACKURITY_ENROLL_CODE = '…'; irm https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent.ps1 | iex
```

Note: The first statement turns on TLS 1.2, which Windows PowerShell on Windows Server 2016 does not offer by default. `irm … | iex` runs the script as text, so the execution policy does not block it. Read the script first if you prefer: it is at /install/agent.ps1 on your Stackurity server.

## What it does

- Refuses to run unless PowerShell is elevated.
- Downloads the agent from your Stackurity server (Windows x64), checks its SHA-256 and installs it to `C:\Program Files\Stackurity`.
- Exchanges the code for a collector token, saved in `C:\ProgramData\Stackurity`. Only the agent's account and Administrators can read it.
- Registers the **StackurityAgent** service. It runs as its own virtual account (`NT SERVICE\StackurityAgent`): no password, no interactive sign-in, no privileges beyond reading, and it cannot write to disk. It starts at boot and reports every 6 hours.
- Its output goes to the Application event log, source `StackurityAgent`.

## Upgrade and removal

- To upgrade, run the same command without the code part, in PowerShell as administrator.
- To remove the agent, its service and its token, run the command below. Then delete the host under **Assets** and revoke its token under **Integrations ▸ API tokens** if you no longer need them.

Remove the agent:
```
$env:STACKURITY_UNINSTALL = '1'; irm https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent.ps1 | iex
```

## Installing by hand

1. Create a collector token as in [Add a Linux server manually](/help/add-linux-server), step 1.
2. Copy `stackurity_<version>_windows_amd64.exe` to the server, e.g. `C:\Program Files\Stackurity\stackurity.exe`.
3. Save the token to `C:\ProgramData\Stackurity\token` and restrict the file to the account that runs the agent.
4. Run it as a scheduled task (at startup, running continuously), as a standard user.

PowerShell:
```
$env:STACKURITY_SERVER = "https://stackurity.example.com"
$env:STACKURITY_TOKEN_FILE = "C:\ProgramData\Stackurity\token"
$env:STACKURITY_ENVIRONMENT = "production"
stackurity.exe agent --interval 6h
```

title: Add a Mac
summary: Developer laptops and macOS build servers: a LaunchDaemon that reads the macOS version, applications, Homebrew and runtimes.
keywords: mac macos macbook laptop apple homebrew brew launchd launchdaemon mdm jamf kandji intune applications
text:
1. Open [Assets](/assets), click **Add server** and create an install command as for a Linux server.
2. Choose the **macOS** tab and copy the command.
3. Run it in Terminal on the Mac, as an administrator (it asks for your password through sudo).
4. Check the Mac appears under **Assets** with its macOS version.

Install command:
```
curl -fsSL https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent-macos.sh | sudo STACKURITY_ENROLL_CODE=… sh
```

## What it does

- Downloads the agent from your Stackurity server (Apple silicon or Intel) and verifies its checksum.
- Creates a hidden `_stackurity` account with no password, shell or home, and enrolls the Mac with the code.
- Installs a LaunchDaemon (`com.stackurity.agent`) that runs as that account, in the background, and reports every 6 hours. Running the command again upgrades the agent.
- It only reads, and needs no Full Disk Access.

## What you will see

- **macOS**: end of life (from endoflife.date). Apple's security updates are not checked, and the row says so.
- **Applications** in /Applications: listed with their versions, inventory only. No vulnerabilities are matched for Mac applications yet.
- **Homebrew** formulae and casks: inventory only, except runtimes such as Node.js, Python or PostgreSQL, which get end-of-life findings.
- **Runtimes and JDKs** (python.org, nvm, pyenv, rbenv, asdf, Temurin, Corretto and others): end of life.
- **Global npm and pip packages**: vulnerabilities, as on Linux.
- Users' home folders are private to their owners, so the agent cannot read `~/Applications` or version managers there: each home folder is shown as not checked, never as clean.

## Many Macs (MDM)

Create a code that can enroll as many Macs as you manage (up to 500) and is valid for longer, then run the installer from an MDM policy script (Jamf, Kandji, Intune, Mosyle); those scripts run as root. A Mac already enrolled only upgrades. A signed installer package is not available yet. See docs/install.md for the script.

## Remove it

Uninstall:
```
curl -fsSL https://stackurity.example.com/install/agent-macos.sh | sudo STACKURITY_UNINSTALL=1 sh
```

Then delete the Mac under **Assets** and revoke its token under **Integrations ▸ API tokens** if you no longer want its history.

title: Add a repository (Git integration or CI scan)
summary: Read lockfiles from a repository, either by letting the server clone it or by scanning in CI.
keywords: git github gitlab lockfile npm composer repository ci
text:
Note: On GitLab, where your server offers it, [Connect GitLab](/help/gitlab) covers a whole group in one step: no token or CI step.

Note: On GitHub, with the Stackurity GitHub App on your server, [Install on GitHub](/help/github-app) is simpler: no token or CI step.

## Option A: the server clones it on a schedule

1. Go to **Integrations** and click **Add integration ▸ Git repository** (admin).
2. Enter the HTTPS URL. For a private repository, create a read-only access token at your Git host, put it in the server's environment as `STACKURITY_SECRET_GITHUB` (any name starting with `STACKURITY_SECRET_`), and enter the secret reference `env:STACKURITY_SECRET_GITHUB`. GitHub needs username `x-access-token`, GitLab `oauth2`, Bitbucket `x-token-auth`.
3. Optionally set a branch or tag, the environment, and how often to run (15 minutes to a week; default 6 hours).
4. Click **Create integration**, then **Run now** to scan straight away. The status shows the last attempt and any error.

The server makes a shallow clone, reads the lockfiles and deletes the clone. Hooks, submodules, LFS and scripts never run.

## Option B: scan in CI

CI step:
```
stackurity scan . --git-url "$CI_REPOSITORY_URL" --environment production
```

- On GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, scan without a stored secret: see [Scan in CI without a stored secret](/help/ci-keyless). Elsewhere, set `STACKURITY_SERVER` and `STACKURITY_TOKEN` (a collector token) as CI secrets.
- Use the same `--git-url` as the integration so both land on one asset.
- For merge-request pipelines use `--name <branch>` without `--git-url`, so a branch that may never merge doesn't replace the default branch's inventory.
- To fail the pipeline on findings, see [Gate CI on findings](/help/ci-gate).

Supported lockfiles: npm, yarn (v1 and Berry), pnpm, Composer, Poetry, Pipenv, pinned `requirements.txt`, Go modules, Cargo, Bundler, NuGet `packages.lock.json`, and `pubspec.lock`. Others (Maven, Gradle, …) are shown as unsupported coverage, never silently ignored.

title: Connect GitLab (a group's projects in one step)
summary: Scan every project of a GitLab group, subgroups included: authorise on GitLab, pick the group, no token to paste.
keywords: gitlab group project subgroup oauth access token webhook push self-managed private repository
text:
Where your Stackurity server offers Connect GitLab (Stackurity Cloud does), you don't need to create a token or add a CI step to scan your GitLab projects.

1. Go to **Integrations** and, on the **Git repository** card, click **Connect GitLab** (admins).
2. GitLab asks you to authorise Stackurity. It asks for the **api** scope once, to set things up; Stackurity revokes that token before the page answers.
3. Back in Stackurity, pick a group you are a member of and click **Connect this group**. Each project appears under **Active integrations**, and the first results arrive within minutes.

## What Stackurity keeps

- As the group's **Owner**, Stackurity creates a group access token named *Stackurity*: **read_api** and **read_repository**, the **Reporter** role, valid for just under a year. It is stored encrypted and can't push or change anything.
- If GitLab doesn't allow a group access token (you're not the Owner, or your GitLab restricts it), click **Authorise read-only access**: GitLab asks for read_api and read_repository only, and Stackurity keeps and renews that authorisation.
- Each scan is a shallow clone that reads lockfiles and is deleted afterwards. Hooks, submodules, LFS and scripts never run.

## When projects are scanned

- Right after you connect, then every 6 hours (change it per project under **Integrations**).
- With a group webhook (Owner role, GitLab Premium or Ultimate): when a push to the default branch changes a lockfile or manifest. Without one, the connection says *scanned on the schedule only*.
- New projects in the group are added, and removed ones have their issues closed as removed (the asset and its history stay), daily and when the webhook reports a change.

## Change or remove it

- **Switch one project off**: open it under **Integrations** and switch it off.
- **Disconnect**: GitLab asks you to authorise once more, then Stackurity deletes its webhook and access token there and stops scanning. The history is kept.
- **Remove here only**: stops scanning and revokes Stackurity's credential without visiting GitLab; a group Owner deletes the webhook later.
- The group access token expires after a year: the connection warns 30 days before. Connect again to renew it.

Note: A GitLab group (and the groups above and below it) can be connected to one Stackurity organisation only. At your organisation's asset limit, new projects wait until there is room; the connection says how many.

Projects in a personal namespace can't be connected: use a [Git integration or a CI scan](/help/repositories). Operators: see `docs/gitlab.md` to set Connect GitLab up.

title: Scan in CI without a stored secret (GitHub Actions, GitLab)
summary: Trust a repository once; its pipelines prove who they are with the CI provider's ID token instead of a stored collector token.
keywords: oidc openid connect id token keyless secretless github actions gitlab id_tokens id-token write trust ci token STACKURITY_ID_TOKEN
text:
GitHub Actions and GitLab CI sign an ID token for each job that says which repository, branch and workflow it runs for. Stackurity checks that token against the provider's published keys and a CI trust you made, and gives the job a collector token that lasts 15 minutes and can only report that repository. There is no secret to store, leak or rotate.

## 1. Trust the repository (admin)

1. Go to **Integrations**, open **CI pipeline** and click **Trust a repository**.
2. Choose GitHub Actions or GitLab CI (for a self-managed GitLab, enter its https URL).
3. Enter the repository (`acme/shop`, or a GitLab project path such as `acme/backend/shop`). To trust every repository of an owner or group, tick **Every repository of this owner**; nothing else matches more than one repository.
4. Optionally limit it to a branch (only scans of `main`, so a branch that may never merge cannot replace the inventory), a deployment environment or one workflow file, and choose the project new repositories go to.

## 2. GitHub Actions

Workflow job:
```
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: stackurity/scan-action@v1
    with:
      server: https://stackurity.example.com
```

Without a `token` input the action requests an ID token for this server and exchanges it. `id-token: write` only lets the job request ID tokens; it grants no access to the repository.

## 3. GitLab CI

.gitlab-ci.yml job:
```
stackurity:
  image:
    name: ghcr.io/stackurity/stackurity:latest
    entrypoint: [""]
  id_tokens:
    STACKURITY_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://stackurity.example.com
  variables:
    STACKURITY_SERVER: https://stackurity.example.com
  script:
    - stackurity scan .
```

`aud` must be the server's URL exactly as the CI pipeline card shows it.

## What the job's token can do

- Report the repository it ran for, identified by its URL (`https://github.com/acme/shop`, or the GitLab project's URL). `stackurity scan` uses that identity by itself; any other repository, host or name is refused.
- Read the result of its own scans (for `--fail-on`). Nothing else.
- It expires after 15 minutes. Deleting the trust revokes tokens already issued.
- Each exchange is in the **Audit log** (`ci.token`, with the repository, ref, run or pipeline id and token id); refused ones that named a trusted repository are logged as `ci.token_refused` with the reason.

## When it does not work

- “cannot request an ID token”: the GitHub job lacks `permissions: id-token: write` (a workflow that sets `permissions` must list it).
- “audience (aud) must be exactly …”: in GitLab, set `aud:` to the URL the card shows.
- “no CI trust accepts repository … on ref …”: the trust names another branch, environment or workflow; the message says which.
- “several CI trusts accept this repository” or “this server hosts several organisations”: set `STACKURITY_CI_TRUST` (the action's `ci-trust` input) to the trust's number, shown as #id on the card; the card's snippets include it.
- “the repository owner's id differs”: the organisation or group was deleted and its name taken again. Delete and re-create the trust if this is expected.
- The server must have a public URL (`STACKURITY_BASE_URL`) for keyless scans.

title: Install on GitHub (the Stackurity GitHub App)
summary: Cover your GitHub repositories in one click: pick them on GitHub, no token to create or renew.
keywords: github app install repositories token organisation private repository webhook push
text:
Where your Stackurity server has the GitHub App (Stackurity Cloud does), you don't need a token or a CI step to scan your GitHub repositories.

1. Go to **Integrations** and, on the **Git repository** card, click **Install on GitHub** (admins).
2. On GitHub, pick the account or organisation, then **All repositories** or **Only select repositories**, and click **Install**. Installing on an organisation needs an owner of it; a member can only request it.
3. GitHub brings you back to Stackurity. Each repository appears under **Active integrations**, and the first results arrive within minutes.

## What the app can do

- It reads the repositories you picked, and nothing else: **Contents** and **Metadata**, read-only. It cannot push, open pull requests or see other repositories.
- Each scan uses a token GitHub issues for that one repository, for an hour at most. Stackurity never stores it.
- The scan is a shallow clone that reads lockfiles and is deleted afterwards. Hooks, submodules, LFS and scripts never run.

## When repositories are scanned

- Right after you install, then every 6 hours (change it per repository under **Integrations**).
- When a push to the default branch changes a lockfile or manifest (`package-lock.json`, `go.mod`, `composer.json` and the like). Pushes to other branches, or that change only other files, don't trigger a scan.
- Repositories you add or remove on GitHub are followed. A removed repository's issues are closed as removed; the asset and its history stay.

## Change or remove it

- **Add or remove repositories**: on GitHub (the link on the Git repository card), under the installation's repository access.
- **Switch one repository off**: open it under **Integrations** and switch it off.
- **Disconnect**: stops scanning, keeps the history, and uninstalls the app from that GitHub account.
- Suspending or uninstalling the app on GitHub switches its repositories off here, with a note.

Note: A GitHub account or organisation can be connected to one Stackurity organisation only. When the app is at your organisation's asset limit, new repositories wait until there is room; the card says how many.

No GitHub App on your server? Use a [Git integration or a CI scan](/help/repositories). Operators: see `docs/github-app.md` to set one up.

title: Gate CI on findings
summary: Make `stackurity scan` fail a pipeline when an open finding meets a threshold.
keywords: fail-on pipeline exit code gate block
text:
Example:
```
stackurity scan . --git-url "$CI_REPOSITORY_URL" --fail-on critical --only-fixable
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--fail-on low|medium|high|critical` | Fail when an open finding has this severity or higher. |
| `--fail-on-priority P1|P2|P3|P4` | Fail on priority instead, which includes exposure, environment and exploitation. |
| `--fail-on-kev` | Fail on any known exploited vulnerability. |
| `--only-fixable` | Ignore findings that have no fixed version (needs one of the flags above). |
| `--wait 5m` | How long to wait for the server to evaluate the scan and prioritise its findings (default 5 minutes). When it runs out the command exits with status 4, “result not ready”, and the gate does not pass. |

- Exit code **3** means the gate blocked; **1** means the scan itself failed, so the pipeline can tell them apart.
- Findings that a security user has suppressed or risk-accepted (with reason and expiry) don't fail the gate.
- Components with no vulnerability source are listed as a warning and can't fail the gate.

title: Import or export an SBOM
summary: Upload CycloneDX or SPDX JSON for software you can't scan directly; export any asset as CycloneDX.
keywords: cyclonedx spdx bill of materials
text:
Import:
```
stackurity sbom import image.cdx.json --asset-name billing-api --environment production
```

- Accepts CycloneDX or SPDX JSON. Without `--asset-name`, the asset is derived from the document.
- `--asset-kind` sets the kind when `--asset-name` is used (default `application`).
- Needs a collector token or an engineer's token.

Export:
```
stackurity sbom export --asset 12 -o asset.cdx.json
```

In the dashboard, every asset page has **Download CycloneDX** in the header.

title: Import and export VEX
summary: Vendors' statements that a vulnerability does or does not affect their product, approved before they hide anything; your own decisions as OpenVEX or CycloneDX VEX.
keywords: vex openvex cyclonedx not affected false positive mitigated cosign attestation
text:
Import:
```
stackurity vex import vendor.openvex.json --source 3
```

- OpenVEX and CycloneDX VEX, also embedded in a CycloneDX SBOM or as a signed attestation (`cosign attest`).
- Products match by image digest, package URL with a version, or CPE. A product that could be more than one thing is not applied and is listed as not matched.
- A **not affected** statement waits under **Approvals** until an organisation-wide security or admin user approves it. Only a source pinned to a public key or an API token can be trusted to apply on its own.
- An approved statement ignores the issue as a false positive or mitigated, only while the component stays at that version (and the image at that digest).
- **Affected**, **fixed** and **under investigation** are shown on the issue with a **VEX** badge and change nothing.

Export:
```
stackurity vex export --asset 12 --format cyclonedx -o asset.vex.cdx.json
```

In the dashboard, every asset page has **Export VEX**, and **Settings → VEX** exports every asset you can see.

title: Import code scanner findings
summary: Findings from code-review security scanners such as deepsec, or any tool that writes SARIF, shown next to a repository's dependency, server and image issues.
keywords: deepsec sarif code review sast semgrep codeql static analysis ai scanner import
text:
deepsec:
```
deepsec export --format json --project-id shop --out deepsec.json
stackurity import code-findings deepsec.json --format deepsec --asset https://github.com/acme/shop
```

SARIF 2.1.0:
```
stackurity import code-findings results.sarif --format sarif --asset 12
```

- `--asset` is the repository's asset id or URL. The repository must have reported first (a scan or a repository integration); an import never creates an asset. In a CI job with keyless sign-in, it defaults to the job's own repository.
- Importing again updates the same findings instead of adding copies. With a complete report, findings it no longer has are resolved as gone. Use `--partial` for a filtered export (for example deepsec's `--only-true-positive`), so nothing else is resolved.
- The scanner's own verdict is kept. A finding deepsec revalidated as a false positive, fixed, accepted risk or duplicate, or one suppressed in SARIF, is closed and never alerts.
- Open critical and high security findings raise one incident per repository and are sent where new issues go. Medium and lower, non-security bugs and rules not tagged as security are listed only.
- `--model` records the AI model that produced the report. The people a deepsec export names (owners, on-call, committers) are not stored.
- Reports are limited to 16 MB and 5,000 findings. Their text is shown as plain text.

Each repository's page has a **Code findings** tab; **Fixes → Code findings** lists them all. A security user can dismiss one that is not a real issue.

title: Scan a container image
summary: The server reads an image straight from its registry with the bundled Syft; nothing in the image runs.
keywords: docker image registry ghcr syft
text:
1. Go to **Integrations ▸ Add integration ▸ Container image** (admin).
2. Enter the image reference, e.g. `ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.4`. Pin a digest (`@sha256:…`) to inventory exactly what you deploy; a tag is re-resolved on every run.
3. Optionally set the platform (`linux/amd64`) for multi-architecture images, and the environment.
4. For a private registry, set a secret reference to the token or password (with **Registry username** when the secret is a password).
5. Click **Create integration** and then **Run now**.

To cover every image in a registry without typing each one, connect the registry instead: see *Connect a container registry*.

title: Connect a container registry
summary: Scan the recent tags of every repository in GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, Amazon ECR or your own registry, and pick up new ones on a schedule.
keywords: registry ghcr docker hub ecr harbor gitlab quay oci repositories tags latest semver
text:
1. Go to **Integrations ▸ Container image / registry ▸ Connect a registry** (admin).
2. Choose the registry: **GitHub Container Registry** (the organisation or user), **Docker Hub** (the namespace and user name), **Amazon ECR** (the region; the keys, or an existing AWS integration) or **Other registry** (its https address).
3. Paste a read-only token or password; it is stored as a workspace secret and never shown again. Or name an existing secret (`secret:NAME`).
4. Click **List repositories**, then tick the ones to scan, or keep **All repositories** with patterns to leave some out (`*-sandbox`).
5. Choose how many of the most recently pushed images per repository to scan (1 to 3), and tag patterns to scan as well (`latest`, `semver`).
6. Click **Connect registry** and then **Run now**. **Images** on the integration lists what it tracks.

Each image is scanned once per digest, so `latest` and `1.4` on the same image are one image, and a re-tag is not scanned again. At most the number of image scans per run you set are queued each run, newest first; the rest follow on later runs, shown as not assessed until then, never as clean.

When a newer tag takes an image's place, it stops being scanned but stays as it was. When the registry no longer has any tag on an image, it is marked **removed**: its issues close as removed and its history stays. A repository that could not be read changes nothing.

Credentials go only to the registry and its own sign-in service. If a registry asks for them to be sent to another host, the run fails with that host's name; for GitLab, set the token service host (`gitlab.com`) on the integration.

title: Connect AWS
summary: Connect an AWS account with one CloudFormation stack: RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, EKS, Lambda and OpenSearch versions, and optionally the agent on EC2 through SSM.
keywords: aws amazon cloudformation launch stack quick create iam role external id rds aurora lambda eks elasticache opensearch plugin managed service ssm ec2 run command agent install
text:
1. Go to **Integrations** and open **AWS**.
2. Choose the regions to read and the region for the stack. Tick **Allow installing the agent through SSM** if you want to add EC2 instances from Stackurity too.
3. Click **Launch Stack in AWS**. The AWS console opens with everything filled in. Tick the box that acknowledges the stack creates an IAM role, and click **Create stack**.
4. Wait about a minute. The page shows the account as connected when the stack reports its role, and the first collection runs.

## What the stack creates

- One IAM role that only Stackurity can assume, and only with this connection's **external ID**, which Stackurity generated. Another organisation on Stackurity could not use it even with its ARN. Stackurity checks this before reading anything.
- Read-only permissions, exactly the calls the plugin makes: `rds:DescribeDBInstances`, `rds:DescribeDBClusters`, `elasticache:DescribeCacheClusters`, `eks:ListClusters`, `eks:DescribeCluster`, `lambda:ListFunctions`, `es:ListDomainNames` and `es:DescribeDomains`. No wildcard actions.
- With agent installs on: `ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation`, `ssm:GetCommandInvocation`, and `ssm:SendCommand` limited to the `AWS-RunShellScript` document and your own instances.
- A small Lambda function that tells Stackurity the role's ARN once, with a single-use token from the link. Download the template from the page to review it first.

## If the account does not show as connected

Open the stack's **Outputs** tab in the AWS console, copy **RoleArn**, and paste it into **Paste the role ARN** on the AWS page. That is also the way when your Stackurity server cannot be reached from AWS. If verifying fails, the page shows AWS's answer: usually the stack has not finished, or the role was changed.

## Install the agent on EC2 instances

With agent installs allowed, the AWS page lists, for each region, the instances Systems Manager manages and which of them already report to Stackurity (matched by hostname). Select Linux instances that are online and click **Install the agent**. Each instance gets its own install code, used once and valid for two hours, and the page shows each result: installed, failed (with the end of the installer's output) or timed out. The instances need the SSM Agent with an instance profile such as `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`, systemd, and HTTPS access to Stackurity.

## Disconnect

Remove the connection on the AWS page, then delete the stack in the AWS console. Stackurity cannot delete it for you.

## Your own role or keys

The plugin also runs as a **Plugin** integration with a role you made (role ARN and external ID) or keys stored as a secret: **Integrations ▸ Add integration ▸ Plugin**, then **AWS managed services**. Its permissions are under **Integrations ▸ Plugins**.

Each service appears as a *managed service* asset; end-of-life dates come from endoflife.date. Vulnerabilities inside AWS-managed engines are patched by AWS and are listed as evaluation gaps, not as clean.

Note: Running Stackurity yourself? Connecting with a stack needs `STACKURITY_AWS_PRINCIPAL_ARN` and AWS credentials on the server; see the install guide (docs/install.md, "AWS managed services").

title: Google Cloud managed services
summary: Track Cloud SQL, Memorystore, GKE, Cloud Run functions, Cloud Run and App Engine versions with the gcp-managed plugin, without a service account key.
keywords: gcp google cloud sql memorystore gke cloud run functions app engine workload identity federation plugin managed service
text:
1. Go to **Settings ▸ Integrations** and choose **Google Cloud** under Sources (admin).
2. Enter the project id and the project number (both on the project's welcome page in the Google Cloud console).
3. Copy the commands shown and run them in Cloud Shell as a project owner. They create a read-only custom role, a service account without a key, and a workload identity pool that trusts this Stackurity workspace only.
4. Click **Create integration**, then **Run now**.

The role has exactly the list permissions the plugin uses; the page shows them. Nothing secret leaves Google Cloud: on each run Stackurity signs a short token naming your workspace and exchanges it for a one-hour token of the service account.

If your organisation cannot use workload identity federation, the page also shows the fallback: a service account key, stored as a workspace secret (**Integrations ▸ Stored credentials**).

Services the role cannot read, or whose API is not enabled, appear in the project's coverage as failed or skipped with the reason, never as zero. GKE end-of-life dates come from endoflife.date; Memorystore for Redis has no lifecycle data there and is shown as not assessed.

title: Azure managed services
summary: Track Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL, Azure Cache for Redis, AKS, App Service and Functions versions with the azure-managed plugin, without a secret in your tenant.
keywords: azure entra aks app service functions mysql postgresql redis subscription consent plugin managed service
text:
1. Go to **Settings ▸ Integrations** and choose **Azure** under Sources (admin).
2. Enter the directory (tenant) id and the subscription id.
3. Open the admin consent link to add Stackurity's app to your tenant, or let the commands do it.
4. Run the commands shown in Cloud Shell as an Owner or User Access Administrator of the subscription. They create a read-only custom role and assign it to Stackurity's app, with a description that ties the grant to your workspace.
5. Click **Create integration**, then **Run now**.

No client secret is created in your tenant. Stackurity's app is shared by every workspace, so each run first checks that the role assignment names your workspace and refuses the subscription otherwise.

Without Stackurity's app (on a server whose operator has not registered one), the page shows the fallback: a service principal with a client secret, stored as a workspace secret.

Windows apps that keep their runtime only in app settings are shown as partial: Stackurity never reads app settings, which can hold secrets.

title: Kubernetes clusters
summary: Connect a cluster with one command: a read-only reporter in the cluster sends its workloads, the images they run, their exposure and the cluster and node versions.
keywords: kubernetes k8s cluster workload deployment pod eks gke aks kind exposure nodeport loadbalancer ingress helm kubectl reporter enroll
text:
1. Go to [Integrations](/integrations) and click **Add** on **Kubernetes cluster** (admins only).
2. Enter the **Cluster name** (e.g. `prod-eu`), optionally an **Environment**, and whether to read the whole cluster or only some namespaces.
3. Click **Create install command**. Copy the **Helm** or the **kubectl** command: the one-time code in it is shown only once.
4. Run it anywhere with `kubectl` access to the cluster. The cluster appears under **Assets** a minute or two later.

Helm:
```
helm install stackurity-reporter oci://ghcr.io/stackurity/charts/stackurity-reporter --namespace stackurity --create-namespace --set server=… --set clusterName=prod-eu --set enrollCode=…
```

The command installs the **reporter**: one small pod in the `stackurity` namespace that reads the cluster with a read-only service account (it lists workloads, pods, Services, Ingresses, namespaces and nodes; never Secrets or ConfigMaps) and sends what it finds to Stackurity over HTTPS every hour. Nothing connects into the cluster and no kubeconfig leaves it, so it works when Stackurity cannot reach the cluster's API server.

The code goes into the Secret `stackurity-reporter`, never into a URL. On first start the reporter exchanges it for its own token, keeps the token in that Secret (the only Secret it may read or change) and removes the code. If you revoke the token under **Integrations ▸ API tokens**, put a new code in the Secret as `enroll-code` and it enrolls again.

The cluster appears as a *cluster* asset with its control plane, kubelet, container runtime and node OS versions (end-of-life dates from endoflife.date). Each Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, CronJob, Job or bare Pod is a *workload* asset, linked to the images it runs (`deployed_as`), pinned to the digest the node pulled.

A workload is **exposed** when a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service, external IPs, an Ingress, host networking or a host port reaches it. An image is exposed when any workload running it is. Risk scoring uses this unless you set **Internet exposed** on the asset by hand.

Running images are read by the built-in image scanner, most exposed first and at most 25 per report by default. Namespaces the reporter may not read (with **Only some namespaces**, every other namespace and the nodes), and images the scanner cannot pull (private registries), appear on the Coverage page as not assessed, never as clean.

## Pulling from the server instead

1. If Stackurity can reach the cluster's API server and you would rather not run anything in the cluster, apply the read-only role from `deploy/kubernetes/stackurity-reader.yaml` (`kubectl apply -f`).
2. Make a kubeconfig for its service account token and store it as a workspace secret (**Integrations ▸ Stored credentials**) holding `{"kubeconfig": "…"}`. When Stackurity runs in the cluster with that service account, set `in_cluster` instead.
3. Go to **Integrations ▸ Add integration ▸ Plugin**, choose **Kubernetes** and set at least `cluster_name`. `environment_label` takes each workload's environment from a namespace label.
4. Set the secret reference and click **Validate and create**, then **Run now**.

Both report the same assets, so a cluster can move from one to the other and keep its history.

title: Fixes
summary: Findings grouped by the one change that resolves them, most urgent first, and what each fix page tells you.
keywords: fix group actions action plan security updates release upgrade kernels needs you hidden snooze my work assigned to me my teams approvals failed checks
text:
**Fixes** answers “what should I do?”, where All issues answers “what is wrong?”, Leaked keys “which credentials must I rotate?” and Automatic fixes “what can Stackurity safely do for me?”. Each fix is one change, such as an upgrade, with the number of issues it clears. The page was called Action plan before 0.6; old links still work.

## The action centre

- **At a glance**: open fixes by priority (P1 to P4), fixes **Overdue** (an issue past the risk policy's fix deadline), the issues the fixes clear, and the issues a newer scan showed fixed in the last 30 days (from [Outcomes](/help/remediation-outcomes)). Click a priority or Overdue to show only those fixes; click it again to show all.
- **The table** lists every fix in one row, in the order you decide in: **Recommended action** (what changes, such as “Upgrade openssl to 3.0.15”, with its kind and a note when it is a major upgrade or needs a restart), **Affected assets** (where), **Risk** (the priority of its most urgent issue, plus **SOS** and **KEV** when an issue matches an SOS rule or is known to be exploited), **Issues resolved** (and, when it clears P1 or P2 issues, its share of all open P1 and P2 issues), **Owner** (who its issues are assigned to), **Deadline** (the earliest fix date; red only once it has passed) and **Status**: **Not started**, **In progress** (someone started, or said they applied it), **Waiting for approval** (someone asked to ignore some of its issues and security has yet to decide), **Waiting for check** or **Regressed** (fixed before and back). Click a column heading to sort by it; click a row to open the fix. On a narrow screen the table scrolls sideways, and a line above it says so. **Detailed** shows the same fixes as cards, with the command and the packages.
- **Views**: built-in ones (My work, My fixes, P1 & P2, Overdue, Exploited) and your own. Set the filters, give them a name and **Save**; only you see your views. The **Assigned to** filter takes **Me** or **Me and my teams**.
- **Select** fixes (engineer role or higher) to **Assign owner** (and snooze or ignore, with the same rules as on a fix's page) or **Check again**, which asks every place that can report on demand for a fresh report.

| Kind | What it means | Typical fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Security updates | OS packages that have a fix in the current release. | `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade` (or dnf/apk), then reboot if needed. On a container image, a Dockerfile step such as `RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y` (or the newest base image tag): rebuild, publish, redeploy, then scan the new image. |
| Old kernels | Kernels installed but not running. Not exploitable until booted. | `sudo apt autoremove --purge` to remove them. |
| Release upgrade | The OS release is end of life, plus OS issues with no free fix in this release and its packages that are also end of life upstream. May say “Ubuntu Pro optional (paid)” when the paid channel has fixes. | Upgrade the release (e.g. Ubuntu 20.04 → 24.04). Ubuntu Pro (paid subscription) can bridge the time until then. |
| End of life | Other software past end of life (MySQL 8.0, nginx 1.18, Python 3.8…). Not raised for a distribution's own package while the distribution release is supported: the distribution still patches it, and the component page says so. | Move to a supported version. |
| Package upgrade | One application dependency in a repository. | Upgrade it to the version shown. |
| No fix yet | No source lists a fixed version. | Mitigate, accept the risk, or wait. |

## My work

**Fixes ▸ My work** (the **My work** button on Fixes, or `/fixes/mine`) is one place to start the day. It lists, each with a count, the first few items, one action per row and a link to the full page:

- **Assigned to me and my teams**: open issues assigned to you or to a team you are in.
- **Overdue**: those issues past their fix-by date.
- **Requests to ignore waiting for a decision**: only if you can decide them (security role or higher).
- **Automatic fixes waiting for approval** (security role, organisation-wide) and **Failed automatic fixes** in the last 30 days. Automatic fixes are part of Stackurity Pro; without it the page says so in one line.
- **Failed checks**: the latest Check again of a fix in the last 30 days that did not clear it (still open, partly fixed, incomplete or expired). A newer check of the same fix replaces it.
- **Open incidents**, SOS ones included.
