A list with nothing in it is one line, such as “Nothing overdue”. **Filters**: **Assigned to** (Me and my teams, Only me, Anyone) and **Deadline** (Overdue, Due within 7 days) apply to the issues; **Priority** to the issues and incidents; **Project** to everything you can see in that project.

## Needs you, and what is left out

| Chip | Which fixes |
| --- | --- |
| Needs you | A fix exists, and it matches an SOS rule or has a P1 issue, on a production asset or one with no environment. The Dashboard shows these. |
| No fix yet | No free fixed version is published. |
| Old kernels | Kernels that are installed but not running. |
| Not production | On assets whose environment is not one of the risk policy's production environments. |
| Lower priority | Everything else: P2 to P4 without SOS. |

Each fix is in exactly one of these, checked in that order. The Dashboard counts the issues in the others, plus snoozed and accepted ones, so nothing is left out without saying why.

## A fix page

- **What and why**: one sentence, for example how many issues it clears and how many are known to be exploited, then the expected impact: vulnerabilities resolved and their share of all open P1 and P2 issues, affected assets, known exploited issues addressed, whether it is a major upgrade (possible breaking changes) and whether it needs a restart (a Windows cumulative update, or OS updates that include the kernel). A fact the data does not cover is left out rather than shown as “no”.
- **Where**: the asset, its environment, the files the issues were found in, and the packages. **Last checked** says when the asset last reported, with the command to check again now (restart the agent on a server, `stackurity scan` for a repository).
- **How to fix**: the command or upgrade with a **Copy** button, the kind of change (patch, minor, major), a warning for major upgrades, and the recommended version from release data.
- **Issues this fix clears**, with bars by priority and by severity.
- **Assign, snooze or accept the risk**: applies to every issue of the fix (up to 2,000; for bigger fixes, act from All issues). Snooze and accept need the security role, a reason and an end date.

Filters (search, asset, environment, kind of fix) are behind the **Filters** button. On an asset's page, the **Fixes** tab shows the same for that asset only.

title: All issues: filters, states and bulk actions
summary: Every individual finding, with workflow state, assignee and deadlines.
keywords: filter state acknowledge assign bulk priority severity verification
text:
**Fixes ▸ All issues** lists every finding. The chips at the top are one-tap presets: **Open**, **Urgent** (P1, not snoozed or accepted), **Assigned to me**, **New this week** and **Known exploited**. Everything else is behind the **Filters** button (a sheet from the bottom on a phone). **Group by asset** lists assets instead: each with how many issues it has and its five most urgent, 20 assets a page. **Show all** opens every issue of that asset. On a phone each issue is a card.

## Filters

| Filter | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Search | CVE, package, title or asset name. |
| Status | Open (default), resolved, or all. Findings resolve on their own when the component is upgraded or removed, and close when the advisory is withdrawn or changed; each resolved issue says why ([Why an issue closed](/help/remediation-outcomes)). |
| Workflow state | New, To do, In progress, Snoozed, Accepted (ignored), **Regressed** (came back after a fix), or **Active** (anything not snoozed or accepted). |
| Fix | Only the issues that one fix clears. |
| Priority / Severity | Tick one or more. |
| Kind | Vulnerability or end of life. |
| Verification | Confirmed (exact version from the package database or lockfile), needs validation (version uncertain, severity withheld), stale (the asset's next report is overdue). Issues on an asset scanned once stay confirmed and show “as of” the scan date. |
| Environment | From the asset's environment label. |
| SOS only, Overdue, Unassigned, Assigned to me, Known exploited only | Quick toggles. |

## States

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| New | Nobody has looked at it yet. |
| To do | Someone acknowledged it (stored as acknowledged); the fix deadline still applies. |
| In progress | Someone is fixing it, or pressed **I applied this** and a check is due. |
| Fixed | The latest report no longer has it. This is automatic. |
| Regressed | It was fixed on this asset and came back. Urgent, whatever its priority. See [Regressed issues](/help/regressed). |
| Snoozed | Hidden until a date or until a fix ships (stored as suppressed). |
| Accepted | Ignored with a reason: accepted risk, false positive, mitigated or no fix (stored as risk_accepted). |

## Bulk actions

1. Tick findings (or the header box for the whole page).
2. Use the bar that appears: Acknowledge, Start work, Assign…, and for security users Snooze… or Ignore…. Other roles get Ask to ignore….
3. A bulk action applies to up to 500 findings at a time; the result lists any that could not change.

## An issue's page

Open a finding to see it in three layers, so the first screen says what to do and the evidence is one click away.

| Layer | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **What to do** (top) | What is wrong in one sentence, where (the asset, and other assets with the same open issue), the priority, the fix and which fix clears it (“Part of: …”), the actions (Acknowledge, Start work, Assign…), and who owns it: owner, state, the deadline that applies and, while a VEX exception waits, who must approve it. |
| **Sections that open** | **Why it matched** (open), **Upgrade recommendation** (open when it means a major upgrade), **Why this priority** (each factor and its points), **Workflow** (deadlines, the reason for a snooze or acceptance, remediation runs) and **Affected**. |
| **Technical details** (closed) | **How this was decided** (source, ecosystem, version rules, matched range), **Evidence** (every recorded fact), **Sources** (each advisory, and related advisories) and **History**. |

Click a section's title, or press Enter or Space on it, to open or close it. A link to a section, such as `/findings/123#history`, opens it. Section ids: `why`, `upgrade`, `priority`, `workflow`, `affected`, `decided`, `evidence`, `sources`, `history`.

title: Snooze and ignore
summary: Hide an issue until a date or until a fix ships, or ignore it with a reason, a scope and an expiry.
keywords: snooze suppress accept risk exception mitigation expiry false positive until fix
text:
Two ways to put an issue aside. Both need the **security** or **admin** role, a reason, and an end. Other roles use **Ask to ignore**, and security decides in the [approval inbox](/help/approvals).

|  | Snooze | Ignore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shown as | Snoozed | Accepted, with the reason |
| Until | A date, or until a fix ships | A date, until a fix ships, or never (false positives only) |
| Where | The issues you picked | This asset, or every asset (including ones found later) |

## Snooze until a fix ships

Choose **Until a fix ships** when no fixed version exists yet. The issue comes back as new on its own as soon as the intelligence lists a free fixed version (a fix only in a paid subscription, such as Ubuntu Pro, does not count). As a backstop it also comes back after the longest exception in the [risk policy](/help/risk-policy), 365 days by default. The Dashboard keeps counting snoozed issues in **not shown here**.

1. Open the fix (to act on all its issues), the issue, or tick several in **All issues**.
2. Choose **Snooze…** or **Ignore…**, enter the **reason** (required), an optional **mitigation** (what reduces the risk meanwhile, e.g. “port closed by firewall”) and the end.
3. Confirm. The issues leave alerts and CI gates until the end, then return as new with an entry in their history.

**Reopen** ends a snooze or an ignore early. Every exception, with its reason, mitigation and expiry, is listed in the [Evidence report](/help/evidence-report).

title: Ignore issues: reason, scope and expiry
summary: Accepted risk, false positive, mitigated or no fix; on this asset or every asset; until a date, a fix, or never.
keywords: ignore accept risk false positive mitigated no fix everywhere scope expiry rule rejected
text:
## Reason

| Reason | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| Accepted risk | You know the risk and accept it for a while. |
| False positive | The issue does not apply here. The issue's verification is set to **rejected**, with your reason as the evidence, and stays rejected until someone reopens it. |
| Mitigated | Something else reduces the risk, such as a WAF rule or a disabled feature. Describe it under mitigation. |
| No fix | No fixed version exists yet. Pair it with **until a fix ships**. |

## Scope

- **This asset**: the issue (the same component and advisory) on this asset, including a new version of the component that still has it.
- **Every asset**: the same issue on every asset of the workspace, including assets and issues found later.

## Expiry

- **A date**, at most the longest exception in the [risk policy](/help/risk-policy) (365 days by default).
- **Until a fix ships**: back as new when a free fixed version exists, or at that limit at the latest.
- **Never**: for false positives only. Other reasons need an end, so someone looks again.

When an ignore ends, its issues return to new with an event in their history. Each ignore is a rule, listed under [Governance ▸ Approvals ▸ Ignore rules](/approvals?tab=rules), where security can end it early. Reopening one issue takes it out of its rule for good.

title: The approval inbox
summary: Engineers and viewers ask to ignore issues; security and admin users approve or decline.
keywords: approve decline request ignore inbox approval policy exception gate
text:
Only the **security** and **admin** roles can snooze or ignore issues. Everyone else sees **Ask to ignore…** on an issue, a selection or a fix. The request records who asked, the reason, the scope and the expiry. Nothing changes until someone decides.

1. Open [Governance ▸ Approvals](/approvals). Security and admin users see every request; a count on **Approvals** says how many wait.
2. Read the request: the issues, why, where and until when.
3. **Approve** ignores the issues that are still open, as if you had done it. **Decline** leaves them as they are. Add a note either way.

Requesters see their own requests and what happened to them. Every request and decision is in the audit log (`ignore_request.create`, `ignore_request.approve`, `ignore_request.decline`).

## Policy exceptions

The [Policy exceptions](/approvals?tab=policy) tab lists requests for a policy gate not to count against an asset, or one issue on it, until a date. Anyone who can see the asset asks with **Ask for an exception** on a policy violation; a security or admin user of the asset approves (optionally with an earlier end), declines with a reason, or later ends an exception early. When it ends, the violation counts again. Each step is in the audit log (`policy_exception.request`, `.approve`, `.decline`, `.end`).

title: Check again
summary: Ask for a fresh report now, and see whether a fix passed, partly fixed or is still open.
keywords: check again verify applied poll agent rescan passed partly fixed still open
text:
Issues close only on fresh evidence: a new report from the asset that no longer has them. **Check again** asks for that report now instead of waiting for the next one.

## Where the report comes from

| Asset | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Server with an agent 0.7 or newer | The agent asks the server about once a minute whether someone pressed Check again, and reports at once. |
| Server with an older agent | The page says: Waiting for the agent. Agents older than 0.7 report on their interval; restart the agent to report now (`sudo systemctl restart stackurity-agent`). |
| Repository connected through Integrations | The server scans the repository again. |
| Repository scanned in CI | Run `stackurity scan` again; the page shows the command. |
| Uploaded application, container image or SBOM | Nothing can report on demand. The asset page shows how to send a fresh scan or upload, and its button says **Check the next report**: it waits for that upload and does not start a scan. |

## The result

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Passed | None of the issues the check was about is left. |
| Partly fixed | Some are gone; the page links to what is left. |
| Still open | None of them is gone. |
| No report | No report arrived within 7 days. |

A check of a whole asset also says how many issues are new. Every check is listed under [Security ▸ Checks](/checks).

## I applied this

On a fix page, **I applied this** says you made the change. Its issues go to **In progress** (“applied, waiting for a check”) and a check is requested. It never closes an issue by itself: only the fresh report does.

title: Regressed issues
summary: An issue that was fixed on an asset and came back.
keywords: regressed came back reopened downgrade reinstall
text:
An issue is **Regressed** when it was fixed on an asset (the component was upgraded or removed) and a later report has it again on the same asset: the same component and advisory, for example after a downgrade, a restored backup or a reinstalled package.

- Regressed issues are urgent whatever their priority: they are counted on the **Dashboard** and sent in urgent notifications and summaries as “came back after a fix”.
- The history keeps both the fix and the return.
- An upgrade that leaves the component vulnerable is not a regression, and neither is an issue closed only because the vulnerability data changed.
- The chip shows until someone starts work on the issue or it is fixed again.

Find them with **Fixes ▸ All issues ▸ Came back**.

title: Incidents
summary: Findings grouped by vulnerability and owner team, plus system problems. Notifications are sent per incident.
keywords: incident alert escalation ack overdue
text:
One CVE across fifty servers owned by the same team is one incident. System problems also open incidents and close on their own: a stale or failing feed, a server whose agent stopped reporting or a scan past its usual schedule ([Servers and scans that stop reporting](/help/asset-reporting)), a failing integration, or an asset whose collected inventory dropped by more than half.

- Filters: status, kind, priority, owner team, **SOS only**, **Escalated** (a deadline was missed).
- **Ack overdue** / **Fix overdue** badges mean the acknowledgement or fix deadline from the risk policy has passed.
- Open an incident to act on all its open findings at once (acknowledge, assign, suppress…), and to see which notifications were sent (security role).

Incidents get an owner team from their assets. Set owner teams on assets (asset page ▸ Edit) so alerts can be routed to the right team.

title: Servers and scans that stop reporting
summary: What Stackurity expects of each asset, what “hasn't reported” means, and how to fix it. Your services may be fine.
keywords: stale stopped reporting not reporting agent offline scanned once one-off as of cadence schedule ci pipeline quiet
text:
Each asset records how its reports reach Stackurity: the **agent** on a server, a **scan** uploaded by the CLI or a CI job, an **integration** the server runs on a schedule, or a **manual upload**. From that, and from its own history, Stackurity works out when the next report is due. These alerts are about Stackurity's view of your systems: **your services may be fine**.

| Asset | Expected | When it is overdue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server (agent) | Every 6 hours | After 48 hours (STACKURITY_STALE_AFTER) |
| Repository, image or SBOM scanned regularly | Its usual gap, learned from its last few scans | After twice that gap, at least 48 hours |
| Scanned once, or only on one day | Nothing more | Never: results stay as of that scan |
| Reported by an integration | The integration's schedule | No alert: a failing integration has its own |

## A server: the agent hasn't reported

**What is at risk:** its findings are not refreshed, so a new vulnerability on it goes unseen. Its last results are kept, marked stale (scored × 0.8). Servers that went quiet on the same day share one incident, which lists the applications on them. It is P3 for a production server.

- Likely causes: the server is off or was rebuilt, the agent service stopped, or it can't reach the Stackurity server.
- Check the agent: `systemctl status stackurity-agent` and `journalctl -u stackurity-agent -n 50`; restart it with `systemctl restart stackurity-agent`.
- On Windows, open the scheduled task (or service wrapper) that runs `stackurity.exe agent`, check its last run result, and run the command by hand in PowerShell to see the error.
- A server that no longer exists: delete it on its asset page.

## A repository, image or SBOM hasn't been scanned

Once an asset has been scanned at least 3 times over at least a day, Stackurity learns how often: “Repository shop hasn't been scanned since 26 Oct (usually every day)”. These go in the daily and weekly summaries only, as P4, unless the asset is production and set to **Daily** or **Weekly**: then it is P3 and told right away.

- Likely cause: the CI job or scheduled scan that uploads it stopped or failed. Check its last pipeline run.
- Scan commands are in **Integrations ▸ CI pipeline**.
- Scanned only now and then? On the asset page, **Edit** ▸ **Expected reporting** ▸ **One-off or manual**.

## Scanned once

A repository, image or SBOM scanned a single time, or re-run only on the day it was set up (from a laptop, or a trial), is **one-off**: no alert, never stale, not scored as stale. The asset page and **Home** say “Scanned once on 26 Oct. Results stay as of that date”, each of its issues shows **as of 26 Oct**, and after 90 days the note says how old the results are. The weekly summary has one line about such assets. To keep one current, scan it on a schedule:

GitHub Actions:
```
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"
jobs:
  stackurity:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: stackurity/scan-action@v1
        with:
          server: https://stackurity.example.com
          token: ${{ secrets.STACKURITY_TOKEN }}
```

GitLab CI (add a pipeline schedule; STACKURITY_TOKEN as a masked variable):
```
stackurity:
  image:
    name: ghcr.io/stackurity/stackurity:latest
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    STACKURITY_SERVER: https://stackurity.example.com
  script:
    - stackurity scan . --git-url "$CI_REPOSITORY_URL"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

## Expected reporting

- **Automatic**: learned from its reports (the default).
- **Daily**: overdue after 48 hours.
- **Weekly**: overdue after 8 days.
- **One-off or manual**: never overdue. Not offered for a server the agent reports: it would never say if the agent stopped. Delete a server that is gone.

Note: A server that reports again for less than a day and goes quiet again reopens its earlier incident, so a flaky agent does not send an alert every day. PagerDuty, Jira and ServiceNow still treat it as new: a new page, issue or record, resolved again when it reports.

title: Assets: filters, tabs, reboot and drift
summary: Everything Stackurity knows about each server, repository, image or service.
keywords: asset reboot pending drift replica relations coverage collections ownership
text:
## Filters

- Search by name; Kind; Environment; Status (**ok**, **partial** – the last collection was incomplete, **stale** – its next report is overdue: 48 hours for a server, twice its usual gap for a scan; an asset scanned once is never stale, see [Servers and scans that stop reporting](/help/asset-reporting)); Owner team.
- **Reboot pending**: hosts running older code than is installed. Patched packages protect nothing until the process or kernel restarts.

## On an asset

- **Edit** (engineer): environment, owner team, criticality, internet exposure, tags (these feed the priority), and **Expected reporting**: automatic, daily, weekly or one-off.
- **Fixes** tab: the fixes for this asset. Above the tabs, the health line says how many need you, and when the asset was last checked with the command to check again.
- **Issues**, **Inventory** (every component; click a row for its evidence), **Coverage** (what was checked), **Collections** (each report received).
- **Relations**: link assets, e.g. an image `built_from` a repository, or a standby `replica_of` its primary.
- **Drift**: compares versions with a primary (`replica_of`) or any asset you pick, showing what is behind, ahead or missing.
- **Automatic fixes**: changes applied to this host, and (admin) **Enable remediation**.
- **Details** (below the tabs, collapsed): attributes, identifiers, owner and context. **Delete asset** is in the **Danger zone** at the bottom (admin).
- **Download CycloneDX** exports the inventory; **Delete asset** (admin) removes it and its history.

title: Components
summary: Every package across all assets, with where each version is used.
text:
1. Search by name or filter by type (deb, npm, composer, …).
2. Open a component to see the latest release (npm and Packagist), its lifecycle (which release lines are end of life, and which ones you run), open findings, and every asset using it.

title: Updates available
summary: Packages behind their latest stable release, with or without a known vulnerability.
keywords: outdated newer release latest stable patch minor major upgrade behind dependencies bootstrap npm
text:
**Updates available** lists every package behind its latest stable release, for when you plan maintenance, whether or not the newer release fixes a known vulnerability. Being behind is not an issue on its own: it gets no priority and raises no incident or alert. An install with open issues says so in the **Security** column and links to them; **Fixes** is where those are put in order.

1. Open **Assets ▸ Updates available**. The counts show installs behind their latest stable release by **patch**, **minor** and **major**.
2. Filter by update type or by asset. **Packages most behind** groups installs per package with the versions in use; open a package for its release data and every asset using it.
3. **Installs** lists each one, with its asset.

- Only packages from a registry (npm, Packagist, PyPI, Go, crates.io, RubyGems, NuGet, Maven, pub, Hex) and WordPress plugins and themes from wordpress.org are covered. Operating system packages, other generic components and plugins updated from elsewhere (a WordPress plugin whose Update URI names another host, a must-use plugin) are left out.
- A pre-release is never the latest stable release. An installed pre-release of the latest release (2.0.0-rc.1 with 2.0.0 out) counts as that kind of release: 2.0.0 major, 2.1.0 minor, 2.1.3 patch.
- To get them in the weekly summary, tick **Include updates available in the weekly summary** on a notification integration (off by default; never in daily summaries). See [Notifications](/help/notifications).

title: Threat notices
summary: What Stackurity tells you when a new attack, attacker tool or exploited vulnerability appears, and what to do about it.
keywords: threat notice artex nginx2root attack tool exploited disclosed vulnerability kev campaign banner found covered connect upgrade feed
text:
When a new attack, attacker tool or actively exploited vulnerability appears (or a critical vulnerability that attackers are expected to target, such as nginx2root), Stackurity adds a check for it and tells each organisation once what it means for them. Administrators and the security team see a **banner** and get **one email**; the organisation's notification rules that send **Threat notices** (Slack, Teams, email) get a message too. You don't have to ask: notices go out on their own.

| The notice says | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Found | The threat's checks found it on your assets. | Press **See findings**. For a vulnerability, apply the fix on those assets, internet-facing ones first. For an attacker tool, find out who installed it and why; if nobody in your organisation did, treat the asset as compromised. |
| Covered | Your connected assets are checked for it and nothing was found. | Nothing. The notice may name another connection that would check more of your estate. |
| Needs a connection | Stackurity can check for it, but needs something from you: the agent on your servers, Docker access through the agent, your repositories, a cloud account. | Press **Connect** for the Help page that sets it up. Once connected, the check runs on its own. |
| Upgrade | Self-hosted only: this server is older than the release that has the check. | Upgrade to the latest version ([Backups and upgrades](/help/backups-upgrades)). Stackurity Cloud always runs the latest version. |

- **Dismiss** hides the banner for you only. It comes back if the threat is later found on your assets: that is the one change you are told about again, by banner, email and your rules.
- A project's or an asset's notification rule gets a notice only when the threat is found on one of its assets, and counts only those. Organisation rules get every notice.
- A server counts as checked once its agent is a release that has the check. Servers with an older agent are listed as needing an update, never as checked and clean.
- Notices give counts and links, never asset names, so the same message is safe for every channel.
- Ask Stackurity and AI assistants answer "are we affected by ARTEX?" with the same checks (`threat_check`), and list the notices you were sent (`list_threat_notices`).

Note: A self-hosted server learns about new threats from a public list that Stackurity signs. Fetching it sends nothing about you, and turning off the release check (`STACKURITY_UPDATE_CHECK=off`) turns it off too. Without it, the server still knows the threats of its own release. Notices are worked out and sent by your server: nothing goes to Stackurity.

title: Coverage, Intelligence feeds and gaps
summary: Make sure “no findings” really means nothing was found.
keywords: feeds osv kev endoflife stale evaluation gap coverage state checked request support ecosystem not checked needs you unsupported resolves on its own no published advisories awaiting verification refresh re-evaluate
text:
**Coverage** (Assets ▸ Coverage) leads with one answer: the share of your components that were checked, and a bar splitting them into **Checked**, **Needs you**, **Not supported yet**, **Waiting for data** and **No published advisories**. Each part opens the components behind it. Below it: what you can fix, each ecosystem found (with **Request support** for one Stackurity doesn't check yet), and every asset, worst first. Open an asset's row to see which parts of its report could not be read; administrators can **Show all scopes**.

The asset page shows three separate things at the top: **Reporting** (is the collector sending reports: reporting normally, last scan incomplete or stopped reporting), **Coverage** (how much was checked: fully checked, partly checked or not checked) and **Security** (open issues, with the P1 and P2 counts). An asset that reports normally and is fully checked can still have many open issues. Each asset has a **coverage state**: **Healthy and recently evaluated** (shown as **Coverage: fully checked**), or one or more of **Failed collection**, **Stale intelligence**, **Partially evaluated**, **Unsupported** and **Awaiting verification**, each with its reason. The asset page shows them above the tabs, the Findings tab says how many components the findings do not cover, and the Inventory tab marks each component as **Not checked**, **Unsupported**, **Stale intelligence** or **Awaiting verification** (filter by **Coverage**).

Components that were not checked are split by who acts, on Findings, each asset's page and Coverage: **needs you** first (a version that could not be read, with the fix for each, or application files the agent may not read), then what **Stackurity doesn't support yet**, then what **resolves on its own** once vulnerability data syncs. The banner is a warning only when something needs you, or when vulnerability data is past its staleness window. A release with **no published advisories** is noted on its row and not counted.

**Assets ▸ Data sources** lists the data feeds: OSV per ecosystem (hourly), CISA KEV (hourly), endoflife.date (daily), and the npm and Packagist registries. Each shows OK, Stale, Error, Never synced or Disabled.

- **Refresh** (engineer) syncs one feed now; **Re-evaluate all** re-checks all inventory.
- **Disable/Enable** (admin) turns a feed off or on. Feeds are created automatically for the ecosystems you have.
- **Evaluation gaps** lists components no feed could check (e.g. a runtime installed outside the package manager). They are never treated as clean.
- The first OSV download for an ecosystem can be large (Ubuntu ≈ 750 MB); allow a few minutes.

title: How Stackurity knows
summary: Why each finding matched, the evidence states, the independent second check, and what a match does not prove.
keywords: why matched evidence confirmed needs validation rejected stale second check disagreed agreed could not check proof exploit false positive missing information
text:
Every issue page has, under **Why it matched** (just below **What to do**), one sentence that says why it matched, for example: “Installed 6.10.0 (from web/package-lock.json, seen 2 h ago) is in the affected range < 7.0.7 of GHSA-xxxx (osv:npm, refreshed 3 h ago), compared with SemVer rules; fixed in 7.0.7.” It names the installed version and where it was read, the advisory record and range, the version rules used, the source and when it was last refreshed, and the fix.

The sentence is built from the rule the matcher stored when it made the finding. It is not worked out again later, so it shows what really matched. The same explanation is in the API (`why` in `GET /findings/{id}`) and in the `explain_finding` tool for AI assistants.

## Evidence states

| State | What it means | What resolves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confirmed | The installed version was read from an authoritative source (package database, lockfile, or a front-end library's exact CDN address, script banner, or licence banner or version constant in a compiled bundle) and is in the advisory's affected range, or its release line has ended. | Nothing: act on it. |
| Needs validation | The match cannot be relied on yet because the version was inferred or has low confidence. It scores lower and is never SOS. An issue the second check disagreed with also says **Needs validation: the second check disagreed**, but keeps its priority, SOS and alerts. | The **Missing information** box says exactly what: a confirmed version, or a person comparing the version with the advisory. |
| Stale | The asset's next report is overdue (a server's agent, or a regular scan). This was true when it was last seen. | A fresh report: **Check again**, or get the agent or CI job reporting. |
| Rejected | A person marked it a false positive with an ignore rule. Stackurity keeps it rejected while the match stays the same. | Reopen it, or end the ignore rule. |

Warning: A confirmed match means the installed version is in an advisory's affected range. It does not show that the issue can be exploited on this asset: the vulnerable code may not be used, or may be unreachable. **Known exploited** means attackers use the issue somewhere (CISA's catalog), not that this asset was attacked.

## The independent second check

P1, SOS, known exploited and regressed issues, and those with an unconfirmed version or an ambiguous match, are checked a second time by separate, deliberately simple code. It reads the raw advisory record and the raw reported version itself, with its own version rules, and compares its answer with the finding.

- **Agreed**: it reached the same verdict and fixed version.
- **Disagreed**: it found something different (not affected, another fixed version, a different package or release line). The issue says **Needs validation: the second check disagreed** and lists what differs, and the **Dashboard** counts it for review. Its priority, SOS and alerts do not change: the second check is deliberately simple, so a mistake in it must never hide a real issue. It stays flagged until the match or the advisory data changes.
- **Could not check**: it does not read this case (pre-release versions, SUSE product channels, Ubuntu FIPS builds, some Alpine versions). It says why. Nothing changes on the issue.

The check runs in the background, a batch every minute, so a new urgent issue can be alerted before it is checked. **Coverage** shows the counts and the latest disagreements, and **All issues** can filter by second check. Every disagreement is logged so it can become a new matching test.

title: Evidence report
summary: A printable patch-management summary for a period, for audits and management.
where: Governance › Reports and audit › Evidence report
keywords: audit report compliance print pdf sla
text:
1. Choose **From** and **To** (one day to one year; UTC days).
2. Read the sections: coverage and assets, open findings by severity and priority, overdue findings, remediation within deadlines and median time to fix, every active exception with its reason, mitigation and expiry, and drift for each replica.
3. Click **Print** (or print to PDF) for a clean light-theme copy, or **Download JSON** for the raw data.

**Remediated** counts only issues fixed on the asset in the period: upgraded, fixed by a remediation plan, or removed. Issues that closed with nothing changed on the asset, such as an advisory withdrawn by its source, are shown on their own line as **closed, not remediation**, with a link to the list, and are never in the deadline share or the median. See [Why an issue closed](/help/remediation-outcomes).

title: Audit evidence pack
summary: One download for your auditor, mapped to SOC 2, ISO 27001 and, with the Compliance add-on, PCI DSS and the EU Cyber Resilience Act.
where: Governance › Reports and audit › Evidence report › Audit evidence pack
keywords: audit evidence pack soc 2 soc2 iso 27001 pci dss cra cyber resilience act auditor controls cc7.1 cc8.1 a.8.8 a.8.9 6.3.3 sbom vex zip pdf compliance add-on
text:
1. Open **Reports** and find **Audit evidence pack**.
2. Choose the period: **Last quarter**, **This quarter to date**, or the report's own dates.
3. Tick the frameworks your auditor asked about.
4. Click **Download PDF** for the auditor, **Download ZIP** for the PDF with a CSV of every table and a SHA-256 manifest, or **Download JSON** for other tools.

For each control the pack says what in it is evidence for that control, and what Stackurity does not show (for example, Stackurity is not an Approved Scanning Vendor for PCI DSS 11.3.2). It is evidence for the controls; it never says you are compliant or certified. Your auditor decides that.

| In the pack | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Monitoring** | Every asset, the hours with at least one report out of the hours monitored, and the longest gap between reports. |
| **Findings** | Open at the start and end of the period, new and fixed in it, and every open finding with its CVSS score and whether it is past its deadline. |
| **Time to fix** | Your deadline for each priority and how many fixes met it, with median and 90th-percentile days. Only upgrades and removals count as fixes. |
| **Exceptions** | Every exception active in the period: reason, who asked, who approved, expiry and how it ended. |

Team and up get SOC 2 and ISO 27001:2022. The **Compliance add-on** (on any paid plan; Enterprise includes it) adds PCI DSS 4.0, the EU Cyber Resilience Act, an SBOM of each asset and the VEX statements in the ZIP. Every download is recorded in the audit log.

title: Remediation outcomes and why an issue closed
summary: The executive summary and the detailed view of Outcomes, and what counts as remediation there and in the evidence report.
keywords: outcomes remediation time to remedy mttr sla resolved closed withdrawn advisory changed superseded not counted executive summary management cto ciso print trend overdue owner team accountability business impact exceptions
text:
## Executive summary and Detailed

**Reports ▸ Outcomes** opens on the **Executive summary**, a short page for managers, CTOs and CISOs. **Detailed** has the full tables: time to remedy, how findings closed, SLA by priority, reopened findings and automatic remediation. Your choice is remembered in this browser. **Print** gives a clean one- or two-page copy of the view on screen, without the menus and filters.

| Executive summary | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Security posture** | Open P1 (urgent) and P2 (high) issues, known exploited ones, issues past their fix-by date, and how many assets are reporting. The same counts as the Dashboard. |
| **Business impact** | How many assets have a P1 or P2 issue, and how many of them are production or internet-facing. A line appears only when the environment or exposure is recorded on the assets; an asset with nothing recorded is said, never counted as safe. |
| **Fixing on time (SLA)** | How many fixes in the period were made by their fix-by date, and how many open issues are past it now. |
| **Remediation trend** | Issues found or reopened against issues fixed, per week (per 4 weeks for windows over 90 days). The fixed issues add up to **Remediated** in the Detailed view. |
| **Overdue risks** | The ten most overdue issues, P1 first, with the asset, the owner, how long each has been open and how late it is. |
| **Team accountability** | Open, P1 or P2, and overdue issues per person or team they are assigned to, with Unassigned on its own row. Each number opens that list. |
| **Exceptions** | Requests to ignore issues waiting for approval, snoozes and acceptances that ran out in the period, and how many issues are snoozed or accepted now. |

Note: Both views count the same way, as the Dashboard and the evidence report do, and both end with **How these numbers are counted**. Incident response times (time to acknowledge and resolve an incident) are not shown: incidents do not record when they were acknowledged.

## What counts as remediation

Every resolved issue records why it closed. Only a change on the asset is remediation: **Outcomes** and the **Evidence report** count those in resolved, time to remedy and SLA, and list the rest apart with a link to them.

| Why it closed | Counted as remediation? |
| --- | --- |
| **Upgraded or fixed**: a newer inventory shows another version, or a remediation plan was verified | Yes |
| **Removed**: a complete inventory no longer lists the component | Yes |
| **Advisory withdrawn**: the source withdrew every advisory behind it (“Ubuntu withdrew this advisory on 27 Oct”) | No |
| **Advisory changed**: the advisory or lifecycle data no longer lists the installed version, which did not change | No |
| **Upgraded but still affected**: the issue continues as an issue on the new version | No |
| **No longer evaluated**: the feed was disabled or the version could not be compared | No |

The issue page and its history show the specific reason. In **Fixes ▸ All issues**, the link from Outcomes lists the issues closed without remediation in the window.

title: How remediation works (and why Plans is empty)
summary: Remediation is off until an admin creates an enabled policy and enrols hosts. Plans then appear for approval.
keywords: remediation plans empty approve lifecycle safety automatic
text:
Remediation lets Stackurity apply security updates for you, within limits you set. **It is off by default**: with no enabled policy, nothing is ever planned, so **Fixes ▸ Automatic fixes** stays empty.

## What has to be in place

1. An admin creates a **policy** that says which packages, environments and kinds of change are allowed ([Remediation policies](/help/remediation-policy)).
2. For hosts, an admin enrols each host: a host-bound token plus the agent running as root with `--remediate` and a local allowlist ([Enable remediation on a host](/help/enable-host-remediation)).
3. Stackurity then proposes **plans**: one package moving to one target version across the assets that need it. Only open, confirmed vulnerabilities with a fixed version are planned.
4. A security or admin user approves or rejects each plan (unless the policy approves automatically). Major upgrades always need an admin.

## Plan lifecycle

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| proposed | Waiting for a decision. Shown under **Needs approval** and as the count next to **Fixes** in the menu. |
| approved | Released within the policy's maintenance window and limits. |
| in progress | Canary assets first, then the rest after the soak time. |
| succeeded | Every change applied **and verified** by freshly collected inventory and passing health checks. |
| failed / partially failed | The first failure halts the rollout; the findings stay open. Rolled back where possible. |
| rejected / cancelled | Nothing (more) is changed. |

## Safety

- Authorisation is checked again before anything runs; disabling or deleting a policy cancels its open plans.
- The agent only changes packages that are installed and in its local allowlist, runs a dry run first, refuses apt changes that would remove packages, and never runs through a shell.
- Rollback: best effort for apt, dnf, yum and zypper (if the old version is still available), manual for apk, revert the pull request for repositories. Each plan shows which applies.
- Repositories are never edited: approved plans become Renovate configuration, so changes arrive as normal pull requests.

title: Remediation policies, field by field
summary: What a policy is, every field, and a worked example for staging and production.
keywords: policy field scope change types approval window canary soak health rollback example staging production
text:
A policy is a written permission: “these packages, on these assets, may be changed in these ways, approved like this, at these times”. A change happens only when an **enabled** policy matches **all** of its conditions. Admins edit policies; security users can view them.

| Field | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Name, Description | For people. |
| Enabled | Off means the policy authorises nothing and its open plans are cancelled. New policies start disabled. |
| Target | **Host packages** (the agent applies them) or **Repositories** (Renovate pull requests). |
| Ecosystems | Hosts: deb (apt), rpm (dnf, yum or zypper, chosen from the host's OS), apk. Repositories: npm, composer. At least one. |
| Components (optional) | Versionless purls or globs, one per line, e.g. `pkg:deb/ubuntu/openssl` or `pkg:deb/debian/libssl*`. Empty = every package in the ecosystems. |
| Change types | **Security backport** (`distro`: same upstream version, only the distro revision changes, the safest), **Patch**, **Minor**, **Major**. At least one. |
| Allow major upgrades | Required for Major; such policies must keep approval required, and only admins can approve major plans. |
| Environments | Ticked environments only; none ticked = all. |
| Owner teams | Assets owned by these teams only; none = all. |
| Asset tags | An asset with any of these tags matches; empty = no tag condition. |
| Minimum finding priority | Only plan changes for findings at this priority or higher (default P4 = all). |
| Only upgrade packages that have open findings | On by default: no upgrades just for being newer. |
| Approval | **Required**: a security or admin user approves each plan. **Automatic**: plans start without approval (not allowed with major). |
| Maintenance window | Days (Mon–Sun), From/Until (`HH:MM`, both or neither) and time zone (e.g. `Asia/Kolkata`). Empty = any time. |
| Canary assets | How many assets change first (non-production and lower criticality first). 0 = no canary stage. |
| Soak time | Minutes to wait after the canary succeeds before the rest. |
| Max concurrent changes | How many assets change at once (at least 1). |
| Health checks | systemd units that must be active after the change, e.g. `nginx.service` (hosts only). |
| Roll back automatically | On failure, reinstall the previous version if it is still available (apt, dnf, yum and zypper). |

## Worked example: automatic for staging, approval for production

1. Go to **Settings ▸ Automatic fixes** and click **Add policy**.
2. Policy 1, “staging security backports”: Target **Host packages**, Ecosystems **deb**, Change types **Security backport** only, Environments **staging**, Approval **Automatic**, window Mon–Fri 02:00–05:00 in your time zone, Canary 1, Soak 60, Max concurrent 5, Health checks `nginx.service`, Roll back automatically on. Tick **Enabled** and save.
3. Policy 2, “production security backports”: the same, but Environments **production**, Approval **Required**, Minimum finding priority **P2**, Canary 2, Soak 240, Max concurrent 2.
4. Enrol the hosts ([Enable remediation on a host](/help/enable-host-remediation)), allowlisting the packages you are comfortable with.
5. Staging plans now run on their own in the window. Production plans wait in **Fixes ▸ Automatic fixes ▸ Needs approval**; open one, check the assets, environments and rollback note, and click **Approve** or **Reject** with a note.

Note: Before automating production: run with approval required on non-production first, deliberately test a rollback, and confirm your backups and snapshots.

title: Enable remediation on a host
summary: Mint a host-bound token, write the allowlist, and run the agent as root with --remediate.
keywords: enable remediation host token allowlist root remediate
text:
Warning: The remediation agent runs as **root** so it can use the package manager. Hosts you don't enrol keep the unprivileged, read-only agent.

1. Open the host under **Assets**, go to the **Automatic fixes** tab and click **Enable remediation…** (admin), then **Create host token**. Copy it; it is shown once. It can only report for this host and fetch this host's changes.
2. On the host, save the token to `/etc/stackurity/token` (mode 600) and write `/etc/stackurity/remediation-allow`: one shell-glob package pattern per line, e.g. `libssl*`, `openssl`. Only listed packages can ever change, whatever the server asks.
3. Install the systemd unit shown on the page: `stackurity agent --remediate --interval 6h --action-interval 5m`, running as root.
4. `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now stackurity-remediate.service`, and stop the read-only agent on that host if it uses a different token.
5. Nothing changes until a plan covering this host is approved. To un-enrol, revoke the token under **Integrations ▸ API tokens**.

title: Two-factor sign-in
summary: Passkeys, security keys, an authenticator app and recovery codes, and how an organisation can require them.
keywords: 2fa mfa two factor passkey security key yubikey webauthn fido touch id face id windows hello totp authenticator app recovery codes phishing email code otp
text:
A second factor means someone who learns your password still cannot sign in as you. Set yours up under [Your account](/account#mfa).

## Add a passkey (recommended)

1. Open [Your account](/account#mfa) and, under **Passkeys and security keys**, click **Add a passkey or security key**.
2. Give it a name you will recognise, such as “MacBook Touch ID” or “YubiKey 5”, and enter your password.
3. Your browser asks where to save the passkey: this device (fingerprint, face or PIN), your phone, a password manager, or a security key you plug in or tap.
4. The first time, Stackurity shows ten **recovery codes**. Save them in your password manager: each signs you in once if you lose your devices.

Add a second passkey or key as a spare. A passkey is tied to this Stackurity's web address, so a look-alike site cannot use it.

## Sign in with a passkey

- **Sign in with a passkey** on the sign-in page needs no email or password: your device confirms it is you with your fingerprint, face or PIN.
- Or sign in with your password; Stackurity then asks for your passkey, a code from your authenticator app, or a recovery code.

## Authenticator app

Under **Authenticator app**, click **Set up an authenticator app**, enter your password, scan the QR code with 1Password, Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator or a similar app, and type the six-digit code it shows.

## Email codes (fallback)

If your organisation allows them and you cannot use a passkey or an authenticator app, **Use email codes** sends a six-digit code to your email address after your password. It is weaker: anyone who can read your email could use it. Setting up a passkey or an app turns email codes off, and admins and security members cannot use them. You get an email each time you sign in with one.

## Rename or remove a method

- Each passkey shows when it was added and last used. **Rename** changes its name; **Remove** asks for your password.
- Adding or removing a method signs you out on your other devices.
- If your organisation requires two-factor sign-in, you cannot remove the last method that counts there: add another one first.

## Require it for your organisation (admins)

Under [People → Users](/people), **Two-factor sign-in** sets who must use it (optional, everyone, or admins and security) and which methods count. On the Enterprise plan, **Require phishing-resistant sign-in (passkeys only) for admins** makes admins sign in with a passkey. You must meet a policy yourself before you can save it.

- People without a method that counts are sent straight to set one up when they next sign in, with passkeys offered first.
- People who have one but signed in with something else (the app, where admins must use a passkey) are asked to confirm with it.
- People who sign in with single sign-on use their identity provider’s second factor instead.
- API tokens and connected AI assistants are not asked for a second factor: review them under [API tokens](/integrations/tokens).

## Lost your device?

- Sign in with your password and a recovery code, then add a new passkey or app and remove the lost one.
- No recovery codes left? An admin can click **Reset two-factor** next to your name under [People → Users](/people). It removes all your methods and signs you out; you then set them up again.

Note: Text-message (SMS) codes are not offered on purpose: phone numbers can be hijacked by SIM swapping, and passkeys and authenticator apps are stronger and free.

Warning: Passkeys work only on the web address they were made for. If your Stackurity moves to a new address, sign in with a recovery code or your authenticator app and add your passkeys again.

title: Risk policy: priorities, deadlines and SOS
summary: How the P1–P4 score is built, the deadlines per priority, exception limits and SOS rules.
keywords: priority score weights thresholds sla deadlines sos rules exception max days epss exploit prediction first patch calendar patch tuesday window due dates maintenance
text:
Everyone can view the risk policy; only admins can change it. Changes apply on the next notification cycle (within a few minutes). **Reset to default** restores the values below.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base score by severity | critical 9.5, high 7.5, medium 5, low 2.5, none 0.5, unknown 5 | Used when there is no CVSS score. |
| End of life | 6 | Base score for end-of-life findings. |
| Known exploited (KEV) | +3 |  |
| Likely exploit (FIRST EPSS) / EPSS threshold | +1.5 / 10% | Added while the CVE's EPSS (the chance of exploitation in the next 30 days) is at or above the threshold, and kept until it falls below 80% of it, so daily changes do not move priorities. Not added for KEV entries; at most the KEV points. |
| Internet exposed / exposure unknown | +1.5 / +0.5 | Set exposure on the asset to get this right. |
| Production environment | +1 | Environments named in *Production environments* (default `production`, `prod`). |
| Environment unknown | +0.5 | The asset has no environment. Set it to get this right. |
| Fix available | +0.5 |  |
| Overdue | +1 | Past its fix deadline. |
| Dev-only dependency | −2 |  |
| Kernel not running | −10 | Idle kernels sink to P4. |
| Asset criticality | critical +1.5, high +1, medium 0, low −1 | Set on the asset. |
| Multipliers | version not confirmed ×0.7, stale asset ×0.8 | Less certain evidence scores lower. |
| Thresholds | P1 ≥ 12, P2 ≥ 8.5, P3 ≥ 6, else P4 | Must be P1 > P2 > P3. |
| Deadlines (acknowledge / fix) | P1 4 h / 3 days, P2 24 h / 14 days, P3 72 h / 45 days, P4 168 h / 90 days | Missing them escalates the incident. |
| Due dates | Days after first seen (the deadlines above) | Or **Next patch window**: P1, SOS and known-exploited findings keep the deadlines above; the rest are due when their asset's next patch window after first seen ends. See below. |
| Exception max days | 365 | Longest allowed suppression or risk acceptance. |
| SOS rules | “Known exploited in production”; “Critical, exposed production asset” | A rule needs more than severity alone. Only confirmed findings can be SOS. Unknown exposure counts as exposed and no environment as production. |

**Patch calendar.** Most vulnerabilities are routine maintenance, not incidents. With **Due dates: Next patch window**, a non-urgent finding is due at the end of its asset's first patch window after it was first seen, instead of a number of days later. Each month has a test window (by default the Wednesday after Patch Tuesday, the second Tuesday) and a production window (by default a week after the test window), each one day in the policy's time zone. An asset is in the test class when it has the tag `patch-window:test`, else a dev, test, uat, staging or qa environment, else such a word in its name; `patch-window:prod` or anything else is production. A finding still open when its window has passed is overdue, as with any deadline.

Deadlines run from when the asset first had the vulnerability. A new version of an affected package (a kernel update, or an upgrade that is still affected) does not restart the clock; an issue that was fixed and comes back later does.

Open any finding to see “Why this priority”: each factor, its points and the evidence behind it, and the policy version that produced it.

Every change is in the **Audit log** (`risk_policy.update`) with the policy before and after, so any earlier version can be rebuilt. Weights that point the wrong way (for example negative points for known exploitation) are rejected.

title: Notifications: integrations, triggers, summaries
summary: A few messages that bring people to the dashboard: urgent alerts, daily or weekly summaries, overdue reminders. Slack, Teams, email, webhooks, Jira, PagerDuty or ServiceNow.
keywords: integrations trigger events rule slack teams email webhook jira issue ticket route channel project asset inherited turn off edit for this project group gitlab urgent summary daily weekly overdue escalation quiet hours digest rate limit connected first scan slack app add to slack add to teams teams app bot code workflows connect jira atlassian oauth reconnect interactivity signing secret link slack account assign snooze smtp ses sendgrid postmark mailgun zeptomail gmail confirm held quota
text:
Everything Stackurity connects to is in [Integrations](/integrations): **Active integrations** with their status and a settings button, and **Add an integration** for notifications (email, Slack, Teams, Jira, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, webhooks), sources (Git repositories, container registries, Kubernetes, AWS, plugins) and AI assistants. The **Delivery log** is a tab there.

## 1. The connection (admin)

- **Slack**: click **Add to Slack**, pick the channel in Slack, and you come back to its settings to choose what to send. The channel shows as "#security in Acme (Stackurity app)", and **Assign to me** and **Snooze** work inside Slack. If the app is removed from Slack, the channel is turned off and says why. **Advanced: use a webhook** still takes an incoming webhook URL (see below).
- **PagerDuty**: click **Connect PagerDuty**, allow Stackurity in PagerDuty, and pick the service. Stackurity adds an Events API V2 integration named Stackurity to that service and keeps its key; you never copy a key. **Advanced: paste an integration key** still works (see below).
- **Microsoft Teams**: where offered, click **Add to Teams**. Stackurity shows a code (it works once, for 15 minutes, only for you) and **Open Stackurity in Teams**: add the app to the team, then in the channel that should get the notifications send `@Stackurity` and the code. The bot answers **Connected** and Stackurity opens the new integration to choose what to send. It shows as "alerts in Security (Stackurity app)". If the app is removed from the team, or the channel or team is deleted, the integration is turned off and says why; **Add to Teams** again to resume. **Advanced: use a Workflows webhook** still takes a Workflows webhook URL.
- **Email (sent by Stackurity)**, where offered: tick members and, if you like, type other addresses (up to 20 recipients by default). Members get messages once they have signed in to Stackurity at least once. Each other address gets one email with a link to confirm; nothing is sent to it until then. The **Other email addresses** list shows who is pending or confirmed, with **Resend**.
- **Email (your own mail server)**: under **Advanced: use your own mail server**, or the only email option on a self-hosted server. Pick a **Provider** (Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, ZeptoMail, Gmail / Google Workspace) to fill in the host, port and encryption, with a note on where to get the credentials.

| Channel | Configuration | Secret reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email (your mail server) | SMTP host, port, from, recipients, username, encryption (STARTTLS by default) | The SMTP password (optional) |
| Slack (webhook) | Optional: the Slack app's signing secret reference, to act from inside Slack | The incoming webhook URL (required) |
| Microsoft Teams (Workflows webhook) | none | The Workflows webhook URL (required) |
| Webhook | URL (HTTPS) | HMAC signing key (optional) |
| Jira | With **Connect Jira** (Jira Cloud, where the server offers it): the site, project, issue type, done status and priorities, picked from lists. With a token: site URL, Cloud or Data Center, project key, issue type, account email (Cloud), optional labels, priority mapping and resolve transition | None with Connect Jira; otherwise an API token (Cloud) or personal access token (required) |
| PagerDuty | Connect PagerDuty, or: service region (US or EU), optional severity per priority | None with Connect PagerDuty; otherwise the integration key (routing key) of an Events API v2 integration (required) |
| ServiceNow | Instance URL, user name (Basic) or OAuth client ID, optional table, assignment group, category, subcategory, urgency and impact per priority, other fields, resolve state and close code, read state back | Password (Basic) or OAuth client secret (required) |

Secrets are never typed into the dashboard. Put the value in the server's environment as `STACKURITY_SECRET_<NAME>` (or a file under `/run/secrets`) and enter `env:STACKURITY_SECRET_<NAME>`. Use **Send test** to check it.

## 2. Trigger: what it sends

- **New urgent issues**: exploited, critical (at **Urgent from**, P1 by default), SOS, or came back after a fix.
- **All new issues**: every new issue at or above **"All new issues" from** (every priority by default).
- **Issues that came back after a fix**, **New asset connected** and **Collection, feed or platform problems**.
- **Fix overdue** (Pro): at most once a day, when urgent issues pass their fix deadline; summaries then also have an overdue section.
- **Daily summary** at a time, and **Weekly summary** on a day at that time. Skipped when nothing changed.
- **Include updates available in the weekly summary** (off by default, shown with **Weekly summary**): adds the packages behind their latest stable release, by patch, minor and major, with the 10 most behind. Daily summaries never carry them. Not security issues: they never raise issues or urgent messages, and send the weekly summary on their own. See [Updates available](/help/updates-available).
- Slack integrations can send each event to a different Slack channel: pick it next to the event (**Same as this integration** by default).

## 3. Notification settings

- Limit by project, environment, incident kind and owner team (none ticked = all), or tick **SOS incidents only**.
- **Quiet hours** and the **time zone** of summaries. Quiet hours delay everything except SOS.
- **Hourly limit**: messages over it are counted in the next summary; without a summary they are sent together, once an hour.
- **Also send when issues are fixed**: summaries list what was closed, and by which fix.
- Older setups can have several **rules** on one integration (for example one per project); each is edited the same way, and **Add another rule** adds one. Jira, PagerDuty and ServiceNow integrations have no trigger: they keep one record per incident, and only the filters apply.

Note: Email sent by Stackurity has limits per organisation (for example 30 a minute, 300 an hour, 1,000 a day). Messages over a limit are held and added to the next summary; the **Delivery log** shows them as held, with the reason.

## Notifications of a project or an asset

Like groups and projects in GitLab, rules and channels belong to the organisation, a project or an asset, so the backend, frontend and server teams of one organisation are not all sent everything. The organisation's rules apply to every project and asset. Each project's page (and [Project notifications](/project-notifications) for its admins) has **Notifications**; each asset has the same under **Details**:

- **From the organisation** (on an asset, **Inherited**, also from its projects): each rule shows **On**, **Off for this project** or **Edited for this project**. **Turn off for this project** stops it sending about the project's assets; an asset also in another project still gets it through that one. **Edit for this project** gives the project its own copy to change (where to send, what to send), and **Use the organisation's rule again** removes the copy.
- **This project's rules**: rules only this project's people need, with **Add rule**. They send to the organisation's channels or the project's own, and only ever about the project's assets.
- **This project's channels**: **Add email** (sent by Stackurity, to addresses that confirm once). **Connect Slack** and **Connect Teams** add the Stackurity app for the project's own channel, when the organisation allows it: an organisation admin ticks **Projects can connect their own Slack or Teams** in [Settings ▸ Project permissions](/settings/project-permissions) (off by default). Until then the buttons are greyed out and say whom to ask. Webhooks, Jira, PagerDuty and ServiceNow use the organisation's stored secrets, so an organisation admin adds them for the project.
- Who: admins of the project (an organisation-wide admin, or the admin role on the project) change these; security can read them. A rule that was limited to exactly one project is now that project's.
- The same message to the same channel is sent once, even when two rules build it. Turning off a rule to Jira, PagerDuty or ServiceNow for a project stops records for incidents only on its assets; such rules cannot be edited for one asset.

## What people receive

| Message | When | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Urgent | At most once per check (every minute), only when there are new urgent issues | Per asset, the new urgent issues and up to 3 fixes that clear them, for example "commmerceblog: 6 new urgent issues. Top fix: Install security updates and reboot (clears 2,913 issues)" |
| Summary | Daily (09:00 by default) or weekly, skipped when nothing changed | New issues by asset, issues fixed and the fix that closed them, the top 3 fixes still open, overdue counts, problems with collection or feeds |
| Overdue | At most once a day per route, when urgent (P1 or SOS) issues pass their fix deadline | How many urgent issues are past their deadline, grouped by fix |
| Connected | When a new asset's first complete scan has been evaluated | "commmerceblog connected: 1,676 packages checked, 412 issues found, 3 fixes need you", with those fixes. Summaries say "1 asset connected, 412 issues found", never "412 new issues" |

Every line links to the dashboard: the asset's issues in **All issues**, the fix's page in **Fixes**, or the overdue list. Resolved issues are never announced one by one: the summary counts them. A new asset's backlog never raises urgent alerts, Jira issues, escalations or overdue reminders; issues found after its first scan do.

## Assign to me, Snooze, Open

Each fix in a message has three links. In Slack they are buttons, and work with a plain incoming webhook: no Slack app is needed. **Assign to me** opens the fix and asks you to confirm, after you sign in; **Snooze** opens the fix with the snooze form ready; **Open** opens the fix. Following a link never changes anything by itself. A route limited to projects opens every link in its project.

## Act from inside Slack with your own Slack app (webhook channels)

Channels added with **Add to Slack** do this already. For a webhook channel, with your own Slack app, **Assign to me** and **Snooze 1 week** work inside Slack: the message says "Assigned to Nirmal" or "Snoozed until 3 Nov by Nirmal" under the fix. **Open** still opens Stackurity. An administrator sets it up once per channel:

1. Go to api.slack.com/apps, **Create New App**, **From scratch**, name it (for example Stackurity) and pick your Slack workspace.
2. **Incoming Webhooks**: turn it on, **Add New Webhook to Workspace**, pick the channel, and copy the webhook URL. No other scopes or OAuth settings are needed.
3. **Interactivity & Shortcuts**: turn it on and set the **Request URL** to `https://<your Stackurity address>/api/v1/integrations/slack/actions`. Save.
4. **Basic Information**, **App Credentials**: copy the **Signing Secret**.
5. In [Integrations, Stored credentials](/integrations/secrets), store the webhook URL and the signing secret (for example SLACK_WEBHOOK and SLACK_SIGNING).
6. In [Integrations](/integrations), add (or edit) a Slack integration with **Advanced: use a webhook**: webhook URL reference `secret:SLACK_WEBHOOK`, signing secret reference `secret:SLACK_SIGNING`. Use **Send test**.

Your Stackurity server must be reachable from Slack at that address over HTTPS. Each person links their Slack account once: the first time they click, Slack shows them (only them) a link that works once, for 15 minutes; they sign in to Stackurity and confirm. After that their clicks act as them, with their role and projects: engineers and above can assign, security and admin can snooze, and people with access to some projects only can act on those projects' fixes. Refusals are explained to them in Slack. Every action is in the activity log as theirs, marked as from Slack. Linked accounts are listed, and can be unlinked, under the account menu, **Your account**; a Slack integration's page shows yours for its Slack workspace.

Note: Without the signing secret the buttons stay links to Stackurity, exactly as before. Each click is checked with the signing secret of the channel it came from, must be less than 5 minutes old and is accepted once.

## Jira issues

A Jira channel keeps one issue per incident. The first time a route matches, the issue is created with the priority, risk factors, affected assets and fix. Later, findings that join or leave, priority changes and escalations are added as comments, and when the incident resolves the issue is commented on and moved through the resolve transition (for example Done). Incidents link to their issue. **Send test** checks the credentials and project without creating an issue. Each issue carries a `stackurity-incident-…` label that prevents duplicates: keep it.

**Connect Jira** (Jira Cloud, when your server has the Stackurity Atlassian app) needs no token: an administrator clicks **Connect Jira**, allows Stackurity on Atlassian's page and picks a site, then chooses the project, issue type, the status issues move to when an incident resolves, and Jira priorities from lists read from Jira. Stackurity asks only to read and write Jira issues, keeps the connection's tokens encrypted and refreshes them itself. If Atlassian stops accepting the connection (the app was removed from the account that connected it, or it went 90 days unused), the integration shows **Reconnect needed** with the reason and issues are not updated until someone clicks **Reconnect Jira**. **Disconnect** forgets the connection and switches its integrations off; to revoke it at Atlassian too, remove Stackurity under Connected apps in your Atlassian account. Jira Data Center and Server use a personal access token (**Use an API token instead**).

A route to Jira can be limited to **one project**, for example a client's own Jira. Its issues then describe only that project's part of each incident: the project's assets, findings, counts and priority, escalations as comments, and links that open in the project. Stackurity reads them the way a member of that project would, so the database itself keeps other projects' assets out. An incident becomes an issue there when the project's part matches the route; the issue is resolved when none of the project's findings remain open, even if the incident stays open elsewhere, and says so if they open again. A route on the same Jira channel for every asset keeps its own whole-incident issue, as before. For several projects, add a route for each.

## PagerDuty

A PagerDuty integration keeps one alert per incident: triggered when the incident opens (with a link back to it), acknowledged when it is acknowledged in Stackurity (none of its findings is new), and resolved when it resolves. When its priority rises, it escalates or new findings arrive after acknowledgement, someone is paged again: a new alert is opened (its key ends in -2, -3) and the old one resolved, because PagerDuty does not page again for an alert that is already open. The severity follows the priority (P1 critical, P2 error, P3 warning, P4 info; SOS is always critical). Every event uses the alert's dedup key (`stackurity-incident-<organisation>-<incident>`, then -2, -3), so retries never open a second alert. An alert keeps the severity it was opened with. **Send test** triggers a test alert (severity info) and resolves it at once.

**Connect PagerDuty** (when your server offers it) sets this up for you. PagerDuty asks you to let Stackurity read and change services; you pick the service in Stackurity; Stackurity adds an **Events API V2** integration named **Stackurity** to it and stores its key, encrypted, like any secret. The key is never shown again. Your PagerDuty user must be allowed to add integrations to the service (an admin, or the service's manager); if not, PagerDuty refuses and Stackurity says so. Stackurity does not keep access to your PagerDuty account: the PagerDuty sign-in is thrown away as soon as the integration exists (or after 10 minutes if you stop half-way). EU accounts are recognised on their own. Stackurity does not create services: pick an existing one.

**Disconnecting.** Deleting the integration in Stackurity deletes its key. Because Stackurity no longer has access to PagerDuty, the **Stackurity** integration stays on the PagerDuty service until you delete it there: the service, **Integrations**, **Stackurity**, **Delete Integration** (the integration's settings in Stackurity link to it). Until then it receives nothing from Stackurity. Connecting the same service again gives its integration a new key; delete the older **Stackurity** integration in PagerDuty.

**Without Connect PagerDuty**, add the integration yourself: in PagerDuty, the service, **Integrations**, **Add an integration**, **Events API V2**, and copy the **Integration Key**. Store it under Integrations, Stored credentials. Pick the EU service region if your PagerDuty account is in the EU.

## ServiceNow

A ServiceNow integration keeps one incident (or record of the table you choose) per Stackurity incident: created with the short description, a description like the Jira issue's, urgency and impact from the priority, and your field mapping (assignment group, category, subcategory, and other fields such as a business service); updated with work notes when findings join or leave, it is acknowledged or escalates, with urgency and impact following the priority; and resolved (state 6, close code Solution provided, or your values) when it resolves. Sign in with a user name and password, or an OAuth client (client credentials). The account needs the itil role, or rights to read, create and update records in the table. **Send test** checks the sign-in, the table and the assignment group without creating anything.

When ServiceNow refuses (an access control rule), the delivery fails with ServiceNow's reason. ServiceNow silently drops fields the account may not write: Stackurity compares the record with what it sent and says which fields were not set. With **Read the state back from ServiceNow**, a record resolved, closed or canceled there shows so on the incident, is in the activity log, and is no longer updated. The findings stay open until a scan shows them fixed. PagerDuty and ServiceNow routes cannot be limited to projects.

**Delivery log** shows every message, its status (pending, held, sent, failed) and errors; admins can retry failed or held ones. A held message says why: the email limit (it goes into the next summary) or the route's hourly limit (it goes into the next summary, or the hourly digest for a route with no summary).

title: Sign in with Google, Microsoft or GitHub
summary: On Stackurity Cloud: sign up and sign in with a provider instead of a password, and how it keeps your account safe.
where: Your account › Sign in with Google, Microsoft or GitHub
keywords: google microsoft github social login sign in sign up continue with oauth connect disconnect link account
text:
On Stackurity Cloud the sign-up and sign-in pages offer **Continue with Google**, **Continue with Microsoft** and **Continue with GitHub**. The provider confirms your email address, so there is no password to choose and no confirmation email to wait for.

## Signing up

1. On the sign-up page, choose a provider and sign in there.
2. Back on Stackurity, enter your organisation's name and agree to the Terms of Service and the Privacy Policy.
3. **Create account** starts your organisation's free trial, with you as its admin, as signing up with your email does.
4. If you signed up with GitHub, Stackurity goes on to **Pick repositories** when the GitHub App is available, so the first results arrive in a couple of minutes.

- Only an address the provider has verified is used. Microsoft: work or school accounts only (personal Outlook.com or Hotmail accounts can sign up with their email). GitHub: your primary email address, which must be verified on GitHub.
- Temporary email addresses are refused, as on the email form.
- An account made this way has no password. To add one, sign out and use **Forgot password** on the sign-in page. Two-factor sign-in needs a password.

## You already have an account

Signing in with a provider never connects it to an existing account just because the email address matches. Either:

- sign in with your password, then under [Your account](/account#sign-in) choose **Connect** next to the provider (you enter your password again), or
- use the link Stackurity emails to your account's address when you try a provider with it. Open it **in the same browser** within 30 minutes. If you did not try to sign in, ignore the email: nothing changes.

## What still applies

- Your two-factor sign-in: after the provider, Stackurity asks for your code.
- An organisation that requires two-factor sign-in asks you to set it up.
- An organisation that requires its own [single sign-on](/help/users-teams-roles) still requires it: a provider sign-in does not open it (its owner keeps access, as with a password).
- Instance administrators always sign in with their password.

Note: Under [Your account](/account#sign-in) you can see each connected provider, when it was last used, and **Disconnect** it. The last way into an account without a password cannot be disconnected.

title: Users, teams and roles
summary: Who can see and change what, and adding someone with exactly the access they need.
keywords: role viewer engineer security admin team password permission view edit decide phone add user scope specific all projects assets
text:
Everyone in a workspace sees either **all projects and assets**, or only the **specific projects and assets** they are given. On top of that, a permission says what they may do there.

| What they can do | View only | View and edit | View, edit and decide | Admin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| See the assets, packages, issues, fixes, incidents, reports and activity they have access to | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Ask for an issue to be ignored or for an exception to a policy gate, and create their own API tokens (never above their own permission) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Acknowledge, start, assign and comment on issues; mark a fix as applied; check an asset again | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Edit assets (name, owner team, criticality, environment, tags) and how they relate | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| See integrations, run them, refresh feeds and import VEX | No | With all projects | With all projects | With all projects |
| Snooze, accept risk on, ignore and reopen issues; decide requests to ignore and policy exceptions; end ignore rules and exceptions | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| See notification settings and the delivery log; decide VEX documents and remediation plans | No | No | With all projects | With all projects |
| Set up the notifications of their projects and assets: turn the organisation's rules off or edit them there, add rules and channels | No | No | No | Yes |
| Write their projects' notes for Ask Stackurity (what the project is, what to leave out) | No | No | No | Yes |
| Manage users, teams, invitations, projects and who has access | No | No | No | With all projects |
| Set up integrations, notifications, the risk policy and secrets; delete assets | No | No | No | With all projects |

- "With all projects": only for someone given **All projects and assets**. With specific projects or assets, these pages are not shown.
- With specific projects or assets, everything else applies to those only. Ignoring an issue everywhere (every asset) needs View, edit and decide on all projects.
- Admin on specific projects or assets adds only their notifications, and their projects' notes for Ask Stackurity, to View, edit and decide.

In the API and in older screens the permissions are named viewer (View only), engineer (View and edit), security (View, edit and decide) and admin. See [Projects and access](/help/projects) for how projects narrow what someone sees.

## Adding a user
